Dosage_Form_and_Route: Sustained-release drug-loaded microparticles (matrix system)
Technology_Role: Spray drying of nanofibrillar cellulose (NFC) to form matrix microparticles for sustained drug delivery
API_or_Cargo: Different drugs (specific API names not reported in abstract)

Pre_and_Post_Processing: Not reported in abstract
Characterization_Details: Microparticles were characterized for size and morphology (spherical shapes with diameters of around 5 μm), total drug loading, and physical state of the encapsulated drug (mainly in amorphous form); specific characterization instruments not named in abstract.
Performance_and_Bio_Assays: In Vitro Dissolution / Drug Release
Performance_Assay_Details: Dissolution tests assessing drug release from NFC microparticles, with drug release curves fitted to a mathematical model describing release kinetics from a spherical matrix; total drug loading determined (assay method not named).

API_or_Cargo: Paracetamol (model compound; also tablets without drug)
Polymers_and_Carriers: Cellulose nanofibers (CNF; microfibrillated cellulose, nanocellulose, nanofibrillated or nanofibrillar cellulose); compared and mixed with microcrystalline cellulose (MCC: Avicel PH101, Avicel PH102)
Solvents_and_Additives: Not reported in abstract
Formulation_Composition: CNF powder and CNF mixtures with MCC, with or without paracetamol (exact ratios not reported in abstract)
Electrospinning_Setup_and_Params: N/A (spray-drying study)
Spray_Drying_Setup_and_Params: Not reported in abstract
Pre_and_Post_Processing: Tablets produced by direct compression and after wet granulation across a series of applied compression pressures
Characterization_Methods: Powder Flow / Bulk-Tapped Density; Karl Fischer / Moisture Content; Mechanical / Tensile Testing

Performance_and_Bio_Assays: Tableting / Compaction / Disintegration; In Vitro Dissolution / Drug Release

Research_Project_Takeaway: Establishes spray-dried cellulose nanofibers (CNF) as a viable excipient for both direct compression and wet granulation tableting compared with Avicel PH101/PH102, yielding slightly faster drug release in direct-compressed tablets despite lower ductility than MCC.

Research_Track: Track 1: Head-to-Head Comparisons (Electrospinning vs. Spray Drying)
Titlu: Comparison of spray drying, electroblowing and electrospinning for preparation of Eudragit E and itraconazole solid dispersions
Autori: Péter L. Sóti, Katalin Bocz, Hajnalka Pataki, Zsuzsanna Eke, Attila Farkas et al.
Dosage_Form_and_Route: Oral amorphous solid dispersions (fibrous mats and spray-dried microparticles; compressed into tablets for wettability testing)
Technology_Role: Head-to-head comparison of spray drying, electrospinning, and electroblowing (air-assisted electrospinning) for preparing rapid-dissolution amorphous solid dispersions and evaluating 3-month storage stability
API_or_Cargo: Itraconazole (ITR, purity >99%)
Polymers_and_Carriers: Eudragit E (Evonik Industries)
Solvents_and_Additives: Dichloromethane (DCM), methanol (4:1 mixture); 0.1 M HCl (dissolution and contact angle medium); ethanol (UV/Vis content uniformity assay)
Formulation_Composition: ITR and Eudragit E dissolved in dichloromethane:methanol (4:1). Nominal ITR loadings: 20 w/w% (1:4 API/matrix ratio: ES_20, EB_20, SD_20) and 40 w/w% (2:3 API/matrix ratio: ES_40, EB_40, SD_40). Polymer solution concentrations (Table 1): 12 wt% (ES), 17 wt% (EB), 2.4 wt% (SD). Physical mixture reference: 20 w/w% ITR and 80% polymer.
Electrospinning_Setup_and_Params: ES: Aitecs SEP-10S Plus infusion syringe pump, NT-35 High Voltage DC Supply MA2000, single-fluid nozzle (0.75 mm ID); polymer conc. 12 wt%, feeding rate 10 mL/g (as printed in Table 1), nozzle-to-collector distance 0.25 m, voltage 30 kV, drying air temperature 25 °C; productivity 1.5 g/h (ES_20) and 2 g/h (ES_40). EB (air-assisted ES): same pump and HV supply with bi-fluids nozzle (0.75 mm ID); polymer conc. 17 wt%, feeding rate 200 mL/g (as printed in Table 1), nozzle-to-collector distance 0.30 m, voltage 50 kV, spray air pressure 1 bar, drying air temperature 25 °C; productivity 42.5 g/h (EB_20) and 56.7 g/h (EB_40).
Spray_Drying_Setup_and_Params: Pro-Cep-T 4M8-TriX spray dryer (ProCept, Belgium); nozzle ID 0.4 mm; polymer conc. 2.4 wt%, feeding rate 150 mL/g (as printed in Table 1), spray air pressure 0.5 bar, drying air flow rate 0.3 m3/min, drying air temperature 70 °C, cooling air flow rate 0.27 m3/min; productivity 4.5 g/h (SD_20) and 9 g/h (SD_40).
Pre_and_Post_Processing: Pre-processing: dissolving crystalline ITR and Eudragit E in dichloromethane:methanol (4:1) to form clear solutions. Post-processing: grinding of fibrous samples prior to USP I dissolution testing; compression of ES, EB, and SD samples into tablets for contact angle measurements; 90-day (3-month) storage at room temperature and 30% RH for stability evaluation.
Characterization_Methods: SEM; XRPD/XRD; DSC; Raman; Contact Angle / Wettability; Gas Chromatography / Residual Solvent
Characterization_Details: SEM (JEOL JSM 6380LA, 10-30 kV, Au-Pd sputtered): ES yielded bead-free fibrous mats (0.2-5 um diameter); EB yielded fibrous mats with some beaded fibers at low diameter in EB_20 due to lower solid concentration; SD yielded spherical microparticles (1-30 um). HS-GC/MS (Agilent 7890 GC + 5975C inert XL MS, RTX-VMS column): residual methanol <1000 ppm (LLOQ) across all samples; residual DCM <15 ppm (LLOQ) in ES_20, ES_40, EB_20, EB_40, SD_20 and 21 ppm in SD_40 (EMA limits: 3000 ppm methanol, 600 ppm DCM). XRPD (PANalytical X'pert Pro MPD, CuKalpha, 4-42/44 deg 2theta): all samples were XRPD-amorphous at day 0 and day 90. DSC (TA Instruments Q2000, 10 C/min, 25-200 C, N2): day 0 initial crystallinity <3 w/w% for all samples (ES_20 and EB_20 showed only Tg relaxation; SD_20 showed mesophase transition at 87.40 C, 0.07 J/g, and cold crystallization/melting indicating amorphous phase separation; all 40% ITR samples showed Tg, mesophase transition ~88.95-89.45 C, cold crystallization 110-155 C, and melting ~169 C). After 90 days, SD_20_90 and SD_40_90 reached 9 and 10 w/w% initial crystallinity, while ES and EB remained <3 w/w%. Raman mapping (Horiba LabRAM 300, 785 nm, 400-1835 cm-1, 41x41 pixels, 1 um step, CLS fit): no specific API-polymer chemical interactions; ES and EB maps were homogeneous, whereas SD_20 and SD_40 maps showed spatial inhomogeneity/phase separation. Contact angle (Dataphysics OCA15+, 5 uL 0.1 M HCl on compressed tablets at 0 s): 40 w/w% ITR tablets showed significantly higher contact angles (lower wettability) than 20 w/w% ITR tablets, with EB values matching ES and SD within margin of error.
Performance_and_Bio_Assays: In Vitro Dissolution / Drug Release; HPLC / UV-Vis / Assay & Content Uniformity; Encapsulation Efficiency / Process Yield; Physical / Chemical Stability (ICH / Accelerated)
Performance_Assay_Details: In vitro dissolution: Pharma Test PTWS600 automated tester, USP I rotating basket at 100 rpm, 900 mL 0.1 M HCl at 37 +/- 1 C; ground fibers or SD microparticles equivalent to 50 mg ITR (n = 3); UV/Vis detection at 254 nm (HP 8453 Diode Array spectrophotometer) at day 0 and day 90. Content uniformity: samples dissolved in ethanol and measured by UV/Vis spectrometry (n = 3). Process yield: gravimetric solid product mass relative to solid starting materials. Stability: 90 days (3 months) storage at room temperature and 30% RH evaluated by XRPD, DSC, and dissolution.
Key_Quantitative_Results: Particle/fiber size: ES 0.2-5 um fibers; SD 1-30 um spheres. Yields: ES_20 71%, ES_40 73%, EB_20 62%, EB_40 66%, SD_20 51%, SD_40 65%. Productivity: ES_20 1.5 g/h, ES_40 2 g/h, EB_20 42.5 g/h, EB_40 56.7 g/h (~28x ES), SD_20 4.5 g/h, SD_40 9 g/h. ITR content uniformity: 100.0 +/- 0.7% to 100.8 +/- 0.6%. Residual solvents: methanol <1000 ppm in all; DCM <15 ppm in ES/EB/SD_20 and 21 ppm in SD_40. Crystallinity (DSC, day 0 -> day 90): ES and EB stayed <3 w/w% (DeltaH110-175 <0.94 J/g); SD_20 increased from <3 w/w% to 9 w/w% (1.69 J/g); SD_40 increased from <3 w/w% to 10 w/w% (3.86 J/g). Dissolution: 100% ITR released within 10 min (20% ITR) and 40 min (40% ITR) across ES, EB, and SD, unchanged after 90 days.
ES_vs_SD_Comparative_Findings: Electroblowing boosted ES productivity ~28-fold (up to 56.7 g/h vs 2 g/h) and exceeded lab SD (4.5-9 g/h), while ES and EB operated at 25 C compared to 70 C drying air in SD. Yields were highest for ES (71-73%), followed by EB (62-66%) and SD (51-65%, lower due to fine powder handling). Although all three methods yielded XRPD-amorphous dispersions at day 0 with equivalent dissolution (100% in 10 min at 20% ITR, 40 min at 40% ITR) and comparable wettability, DSC and Raman mapping showed amorphous phase separation in SD (attributed to drying above polymer Tg), leading to 9-10 wt% recrystallization after 90 days, whereas ES and EB maintained homogeneous mixing and <3% crystallinity.
Limitations_and_Research_Gaps: Single-nozzle ES throughput is low (1.5-2 g/h), necessitating air-assistance (EB) and multi-spinneret scale-up; EB_20 produced some beaded fibers due to low solution solid content; at 40% ITR (above the cited 7.07% w/w theoretical miscibility limit), ES_40 and EB_40 still showed mesophase transition and cold crystallization in DSC (submicron phase separation); stability was tested only for 90 days at room temperature / 30% RH (no accelerated ICH conditions), and XRPD could not detect the 9-10% crystallinity found by DSC; fibrous mats required grinding before USP I dissolution and downstream tabletability was not evaluated.
Research_Project_Takeaway: Electroblowing bridges the throughput gap of electrospinning (~28x higher productivity at 56.7 g/h) while matching its room-temperature homogeneous amorphous solid dispersion quality and 90-day physical stability, outperforming 70 C spray drying which suffers amorphous phase separation and ~10 wt% recrystallization despite identical initial dissolution.

Autori: Xingzhong Zhang, Yan Li, Jing Li, Hongshan Liang, Yijie Chen et al.
Dosage_Form_and_Route: Pickering Emulsion / Microencapsulation (Food–Pharma Model Overlap)
Technology_Role: Spray drying of O/W Pickering emulsions stabilized by bacterial cellulose nanofibrils (BCNFs) and heat-induced soy protein isolate (HSPI) to obtain edible oil powders (electrospinning not used).
API_or_Cargo: Edible oil (liquid oil microencapsulation cargo)
Polymers_and_Carriers: Heat-induced soy protein isolate (HSPI); Bacterial cellulose nanofibrils (BCNFs)
Solvents_and_Additives: Water (O/W emulsion continuous phase); Beeswax (2 wt%)
Formulation_Composition: O/W Pickering emulsions formulated with 0.1–0.2 wt% BCNFs, 2 wt% HSPI, 2 wt% beeswax, and 10–20% oil phase ratios (yielding spray-dried oil powders of 35.9–56.8%).
Electrospinning_Setup_and_Params: N/A (not used)
Spray_Drying_Setup_and_Params: Spray drying of BCNF/HSPI-stabilized O/W Pickering emulsions; specific inlet/outlet temperatures, feed rate, and nozzle parameters not reported in abstract.
Pre_and_Post_Processing: Pre-processing: fabrication of O/W Pickering emulsions stabilized by heat-induced soy protein isolate and BCNFs with beeswax. Post-processing: not reported in abstract.
Characterization_Methods: Powder Flow / Bulk-Tapped Density; Karl Fischer / Moisture Content
Characterization_Details: Emulsions (0.2 wt% BCNFs, 2 wt% HSPI) showed homogeneous droplet sizes (<1 µm) with narrow distributions and no obvious aggregates across 10–20% oil ratios; spray-dried powders showed hollow smooth spherical structure, improved moisture content, flowability, and bulk density (specific microscopy/sizing instruments not named in abstract).
Performance_and_Bio_Assays: Encapsulation Efficiency / Process Yield
Performance_Assay_Details: Encapsulation efficiency improved by tuning BCNF content and oil-to-water ratios; in vitro lipid hydrolysis/digestibility evaluation showed BCNFs partially inhibited lipid hydrolysis, with minimum released free fatty acid (FFA) values of 72.5% at 0.1 wt% BCNFs.
Key_Quantitative_Results: Emulsion droplet size <1 µm at 0.2 wt% BCNFs + 2 wt% HSPI; oil powder yield/content 35.9–56.8%; optimum anti-digestibility at 0.1 wt% BCNFs with minimum released FFA = 72.5%.
ES_vs_SD_Comparative_Findings: N/A (spray drying of BCNF-stabilized Pickering emulsions only; no electrospinning).
Limitations_and_Research_Gaps: Food-grade edible oil model rather than pharmaceutical API; specific spray-drying operating parameters, exact encapsulation efficiency percentages, and analytical instruments are not reported in the abstract.
Research_Project_Takeaway: Demonstrates bacterial cellulose nanofibrils as synergistic Pickering stabilizers that improve spray-dried powder flowability, bulk density, encapsulation efficiency, and lipid digestion resistance for liquid hydrophobic cargos.

Research_Track: Track 1: Head-to-Head Comparisons (Electrospinning vs. Spray Drying)
Titlu: Preparation and comparison of spray dried and electrospun bioresorbable drug delivery systems
Autori: Péter L. Sóti, Zsombor Kristóf Nagy, Geert Serneels, Balázs Vajna, Attila Farkas et al.
Dosage_Form_and_Route: Bioresorbable sustained-release microparticles and nonwoven nanofiber mats (milled forms noted by authors as suitable for subcutaneous injection)
Technology_Role: Head-to-head comparison of spray drying and electrospinning for preparing sustained-release bioresorbable PLGA/PLA formulations of a highly water-soluble drug (caffeine), with at-line Raman PAT monitoring for spray drying
API_or_Cargo: Caffeine (model highly water-soluble drug)
Polymers_and_Carriers: PLGA (PURASORB PDLG 5004, 50% D,L-lactide, Mw = 40,000, inherent viscosity 0.4 dL/g at 25 C); PLA (PURASORB PL 24 homopolymer, D isomer < 5%)
Solvents_and_Additives: Dichloromethane (CH2Cl2) for spray drying; chloroform (CHCl3) and N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF) (6:1 co-solvent system) for electrospinning; distilled water (dissolution medium)
Formulation_Composition: Spray drying (in CH2Cl2): 5% (w/v) PLGA with 0, 5, 10, 20, 25, 30, 40, 50, 60, 80 w/w% caffeine (plus 100% caffeine SD_CAF; text mentions 0-100 w/w%); 1% (w/v) PLA with 0, 5, 10, 20, 50, 80 w/w% caffeine. Electrospinning (in CHCl3:DMF 6:1): 4, 6, and 10 w/w% neat PLA solutions for diameter optimization; drug-loaded fibers prepared from 4 w/w% PLA with 10, 20, or 50 w/w% caffeine (ES_PLA10, ES_PLA20, ES_PLA50; polymer:caffeine listed as 1:1, 4:1, 10:1 in Table 3 and 50:50, 80:20, 90:10 in Table 1).
Electrospinning_Setup_and_Params: Aitecs SEP-10S Plus infusion syringe pump (Lithuania); NT-35 High Voltage DC Supply MA2000 (Hungary); spinneret ID 0.4 mm; voltage 20-30 kV; collector distance 23 cm; feed rate 0.13 mL/min; aluminum foil collector at room temperature (24 +/- 2 C); productivity not reported in source.
Spray_Drying_Setup_and_Params: Pro-Cep-T 4M8-TriX spray dryer (ProCept, Belgium); 0.4 mm two-fluid nozzle; atomization air pressure 1 bar; inlet air temperature 40 C; outlet air temperature 38 C; pump feed rate 2.24 mL/min; drying airflow 0.8 m3/min; productivity not reported in source.
Pre_and_Post_Processing: Pre-processing: dissolving PLGA (5% w/v) or PLA (1% w/v) in CH2Cl2 with caffeine for SD, and PLA (4, 6, 10 w/w%) in CHCl3:DMF (6:1) with caffeine for ES. Post-processing: vacuum drying of samples prior to SEM; milling mentioned only conceptually for future subcutaneous injection.
Characterization_Details: SEM (JEOL JSM 6380LA, 10-30 kV, Au/Ag sputtered; 200 fibers measured): SD PLA spheres were 3-10 um, becoming distorted/doughnut-like at high caffeine loading (SD_PLA50); ES neat PLA fiber diameters decreased with polymer concentration from 2346 +/- 718 nm (10 w/w%) to 2038 +/- 723 nm (6 w/w%) and 817 +/- 172 nm (4 w/w%), while caffeine increased 4 w/w% PLA fibers to 971 +/- 358 nm (ES_PLA10, smooth), 996 +/- 362 nm (ES_PLA20), and 1012 +/- 367 nm (ES_PLA50, rough surface). Polarized microscopy (Amplival Carl Zeiss, 100x): ES_PLA50 showed colorful birefringent crystals, whereas ES_PLA10 appeared crystal-free. DSC (SETARAM DSC 92, 10-20 mg, 1.6 bar N2, 10 C/min, 30-300 C): PLGA Tg ~60 C; caffeine Form II-to-I transition at 145 C and melting at 234-239 C; melting endotherm disappeared below 10% caffeine in SD_PLGA, between 10-20% in SD_PLA, and at 10% in ES_PLA10; fast drying caused PLA Tg + cold crystallization enthalpy change at 60-80 C. XRD (PANalytical X'pert Pro MPD, CuKalpha, 2/4-42 deg 2theta): SD amorphized caffeine only at 5% loading (SD_PLA5, SD_PLGA5), whereas ES achieved amorphization at 10% (ES_PLA10); 50% loading remained crystalline in both. At-line Raman PAT (LabRAM 300, 785 nm probe, 500-1800 cm-1, 25 points/sample, 2-LV PLS): caffeine bands at 1328 and 555 cm-1, lactate at 1769 cm-1, PLA at 872 cm-1; Raman mapping (532 nm Nd-YAG, 41x41 pixels, 1 um step) showed phase inhomogeneity in SD_PLA5 and SD_PLA10 vs homogeneous drug distribution in ES_PLA10.
Performance_and_Bio_Assays: In Vitro Dissolution / Drug Release; Encapsulation Efficiency / Process Yield
Performance_Assay_Details: In vitro release: Erweka DT6 dissolution tester in 900 mL distilled water at 37 +/- 1 C, 50 rpm; solid dispersions (~10 mg caffeine) placed in a spherical wire mesh dipped into the bath to ensure complete surface wetting; 5 mL aliquots sampled at intervals and analyzed by UV spectrophotometry at 274 nm (HP 8452A Diode Array UV/Vis spectrophotometer). Process yield: gravimetric ratio of collected solid product to starting solid materials. At-line Raman PAT checked caffeine mass fraction in SD batches.
Key_Quantitative_Results: Yields: ES 94-97% (ES_PLA 94%, ES_PLA10 95%, ES_PLA20 95%, ES_PLA50 97%) vs SD 35-79% (SD_PLA series 54-79%, SD_PLGA series 35-76%). Sizes: SD PLA microspheres 3-10 um; ES fibers 817-2346 nm (neat PLA) and 971-1012 nm (drug-loaded 4 w/w% PLA). Raman PLS predictions: PLGA-caffeine R2C=0.978, R2CV=0.970, R2pred=0.974, RMSEC=4.83, RMSECV=6.17, RMSEP=6.28 m/m%; PLA-caffeine R2C=0.957, R2CV=0.892, R2pred=0.958, RMSEC=6.61, RMSECV=10.59, RMSEP=4.60 m/m%. Amorphization limit (XRD): 5 w/w% for SD vs 10 w/w% for ES. Dissolution: SD_PLGA released total drug in ~3 h (12 h for SD_PLGA5); 50% caffeine PLA samples showed burst release (slower for ES_PLA50 than SD_PLA50); amorphous SD_PLA5 released over 2 weeks, while amorphous ES_PLA10 eliminated burst release and achieved total dissolution over 4 weeks with near-zero-order kinetics.
ES_vs_SD_Comparative_Findings: Electrospinning achieved higher yields (94-97% vs 35-79% for SD), produced continuous nonwoven mats easier to handle than fine SD powders, and operated at room temperature (24 +/- 2 C vs 40 C inlet / 38 C outlet in SD). Faster solvent evaporation from high-surface-area ES fibers and restricted diffusion in oriented polymer chains doubled the caffeine XRD-amorphization threshold (10 w/w% in ES_PLA10 vs 5 w/w% in SD_PLA5) and prevented spatial phase separation observed in SD Raman maps. Consequently, ES_PLA10 delivered burst-free, near-zero-order release over 4 weeks compared to 2 weeks for SD_PLA5. However, SD is pharmaceutically established and was integrated with at-line Raman PAT, whereas ES scale-up remains challenging.
Limitations_and_Research_Gaps: Amorphization and burst-free sustained release of highly water-soluble caffeine were limited to low drug loadings (<=10 w/w% for ES, <=5 w/w% for SD), with 20-50% loadings crystallizing and causing burst release; different solvents were used for SD (CH2Cl2) vs ES (CHCl3:DMF 6:1) and residual solvents were not quantified; at-line Raman PAT was applied only to SD (not ES), and ES/SD hourly throughput (g/h) was not reported; PLGA was not electrospun; storage stability, milling, injectability, and in vivo performance were not evaluated.
Research_Project_Takeaway: Room-temperature electrospinning of PLA nanofibers doubles the amorphization limit of highly water-soluble caffeine compared to spray drying (10 vs. 5 w/w%), eliminates burst release, and achieves 4-week near-zero-order sustained release at 94-97% yield, whereas spray drying offers established scalability and at-line Raman PAT control with lower yields and spatial phase separation.

Autori: Edina Szabó, Petra Záhonyi, Dániel Brecska, Dorián László Galata, Lilla Alexandra Mészáros et al.
Dosage_Form_and_Route: Oral amorphous solid dispersion (ASD) fibers and powders (immediate-release, suitable for downstream blending/tableting)
Technology_Role: Head-to-head comparison of continuous high-speed electrospinning (ES), rotary spray drying (SD), electrospraying (ESY), and film casting (FC) on the same multifunctional apparatus to evaluate how drying rate, morphology, and electrostatic forces affect trace crystallinity and dissolution.
API_or_Cargo: Spironolactone (SPIR, micronized Form II, mp 211 °C)
Polymers_and_Carriers: Poly(vinylpyrrolidone-co-vinyl acetate) (PVPVA64, Kollidon VA64)
Solvents_and_Additives: Dichloromethane (DCM) and absolute ethanol (EtOH) solvent mixture; no hydrogen-bond donor additives (deliberately non-interacting SPIR-PVPVA64 system)
Formulation_Composition: Dry solid ratio of 40% SPIR and 60% PVPVA64. Exact Table 1 feed weights/solvent ratios are not reproduced in the extracted PMC text, except that SD and ESY used half the solution solid concentration (lower viscosity, twice the solvent) of ES to maintain the same ~70 g/h solid production rate. Film casting (FC) used a SPIR-PVPVA64 solution cast into 3 × 50 × 50 mm3 silicone molds.
Electrospinning_Setup_and_Params: Multifunctional continuous apparatus with round stainless-steel spinneret (d_spinneret = 34 mm, d_orifice = 330 μm) at 40,000 rpm; grounded stainless-steel bottom cone with automated air knives and cyclone collection; Watson-Marlow peristaltic pump at 300 mL/h; +40 kV DC voltage; ambient temperature (25 °C) and 45 ± 5% RH. Electrospraying (ESY) used the same apparatus, 40,000 rpm, 40 kV voltage, and the dilute SD feed parameters (600 mL/h).
Spray_Drying_Setup_and_Params: Same multifunctional apparatus operated as a rotary spray dryer: stainless-steel spinneret (d_spinneret = 34 mm, d_orifice = 330 μm) at 40,000 rpm; 0 kV (no electrostatic force); Watson-Marlow peristaltic pump at 600 mL/h; ambient temperature (25 °C) and 45 ± 5% RH; automated air knives and cyclone collection.
Pre_and_Post_Processing: 3-day room-temperature post-drying prior to DSC/XRPD/TGA; ES product pushed/ground through a 0.8 mm sieve; FC film (70 ± 5 μm thickness after 3-day RT drying) ground through the same 0.8 mm sieve; pastilles (~1.5 mm thick, 12 mm diameter, 100 mg sample) pressed at 50 bar (Camilla OL95) for Raman mapping and 0.1 N HCl droplet contact tests.
Characterization_Methods: SEM; XRPD/XRD; DSC; TGA; Raman; Particle Size (Laser Diffraction / DLS)
Characterization_Details: SEM (JEOL JSM 6380LA, 10 kV, Au-sputtered); XRPD (PANalytical X'pert Pro MPD, Cu Kα, 40 kV, 30 mA, 2θ 4–44°); DSC (Setaram DSC 92, 25–250 °C at 10 °C/min, N2 50 mL/min); TGA (TA Q5000, 25–250 °C at 10 °C/min, N2 25 mL/min) plus 90-min atmospheric mass-loss tracking at 25 °C (Sartorius analytical balance); laser diffraction (Malvern Mastersizer 2000, 1.5 bar, 75% feed); polarized light optical microscopy (Amplival Carl Zeiss, silicon oil dispersion); confocal Raman spectroscopy and mapping (Horiba Jobin Yvon LabRAM, 785 nm laser, 570–1765 cm-1, 41 × 41 points at 5 μm step with CLS chemometrics, Linkam THMS600 heating stage 25–250 °C, and 20 μL 0.1 N HCl pastille contact test).
Performance_and_Bio_Assays: In Vitro Dissolution / Drug Release; HPLC / UV-Vis / Assay & Content Uniformity; Encapsulation Efficiency / Process Yield
Performance_Assay_Details: In vitro dissolution via Pharma Test PTWS 600 tapped basket method (50 rpm, 900 mL 0.1 N HCl, 37 ± 0.5 °C, 50 mg SPIR equivalent, n = 3) coupled online to an Agilent 8453 UV-Vis spectrophotometer (243 nm); in situ dissolution precipitation monitoring with an Olympus A50372A borescope (5 mm OD, 0° view); process yield and continuous throughput quantification.
Key_Quantitative_Results: Both ES and SD achieved ~70% yield and ~70 g/h productivity. SEM average diameters: ES fibers 1.27 ± 0.59 μm; SD particles 13.13 ± 6.25 μm; ESY particles 6.48 ± 3.89 μm. Laser diffraction d(0.5): ground ES 10.533 μm, SD 10.766 μm. DSC and XRPD indicated bulk amorphous ASDs (absence of 211 °C SPIR melting peak; thermal decomposition to canrenone at 223 °C for ES and 227 °C for SD). ES fibers dissolved to nearly 100% (ESY particles approached ES fibers), whereas SD plateaued within 10 min at the level of micronized crystalline SPIR due to rapid precipitation/recrystallization (confirmed by borescope turbidity and crystalline SPIR Raman peak at 1690 cm-1 on HCl contact), and FC dissolved below crystalline SPIR. Polarized microscopy and Raman mapping (CLS) detected 5–7% local crystalline SPIR traces in SD particles vs. <1% (comparable to CLS model error) in ES fibers. Post-production residual solvent weight-loss rate over the first 20 min at 25 °C was 0.125 w/w%/min (ES) vs. 0.09 w/w%/min (SD).
ES_vs_SD_Comparative_Findings: Operated on the same continuous rotary apparatus at matched ~70 g/h throughput and 25 °C, ES formed 1.27 μm fibers with faster solvent evaporation (0.125 vs. 0.09 w/w%/min), <1% local crystallinity, and ~100% dissolution, whereas SD required twice the solvent (600 vs. 300 mL/h at half concentration), formed 13.13 μm particles with 5–7% local crystalline traces hidden from bulk DSC/XRPD, and precipitated immediately in 0.1 N HCl. Electrospraying (40 kV on the dilute SD feed) yielded 6.48 μm particles that avoided precipitation, proving electrostatic forces and rapid drying prevent nucleation in non-interacting ASDs.
Limitations_and_Research_Gaps: No ICH or long-term storage stability testing was performed; ~30% material loss from drying-chamber wall sticking in short runs; 3-day ambient post-drying was used without GC residual DCM/EtOH quantification; downstream tableting of ES vs. SD was not tested experimentally; exact Table 1 feed weights/solvent ratios were absent from the extracted PMC text.
Research_Project_Takeaway: Landmark Track 1 study demonstrating that bulk DSC/XRPD fail to detect 5–7% local crystalline nuclei in spray-dried non-interacting ASDs (SPIR/PVPVA64) that cause rapid dissolution precipitation, whereas high-speed electrospinning at matched ~70 g/h productivity achieves complete amorphization and ~100% release.

Key_Quantitative_Results: Only TOCNF at 1.5 mmol COOH/g and 1% w/v sprayed smoothly without pump blockage (0.5, 1.0, and 1.3 mmol COOH/g formed aggregates). Dry MS CE diameters: 2.3 ± 0.5 μm (TOCNF MS, 'ball of wool' morphology), 3.4 ± 2.1 μm (bPEI-TOCNF MS), 3.1 ± 1.7 μm (bPEI-TOCNF@CA70 MS), and 4.0 ± 1.5 μm (bPEI-TOCNF@CA140 MS). ATR-FTIR (1722 → 1648 cm-1) and 13C CP-MAS NMR (165 ppm amide carbon) confirmed covalent amide bond formation during SD. Crystallinity index decreased from 73.6% (pristine TOCNF) to 65.7% (TOCNF MS) and 66.4% (bPEI-TOCNF@CA140 MS). Zeta potential shifted from -60 ± 1.8 mV (pristine TOCNF) and -37.5 ± 0.5 mV (TOCNF MS) to +27.6 ± 1.5 mV (bPEI-TOCNF), +19.2 ± 1.4 mV (@CA70), and +24.3 ± 0.9 mV (@CA140). Swelling in SGF: 248 ± 4% (TOCNF) vs. 462 ± 60%, 500 ± 95%, and 460 ± 140% (crosslinked MS); CA-modified MS exceeded 800% swelling at pH 11. TC loading efficiency jumped from 0% (TOCNF MS) to 70% (7% loading capacity) for all bPEI-crosslinked MS. Cumulative TC release: ~5% at pH 7.5 over 48 h; >40% at pH 2 and pH 5 (32% and 15% at 1 h); in SGF, 44% (1 h) / 52% (48 h) for bPEI-TOCNF MS and 50% (1 h) / 60% (48 h) for both CA-modified MS. Kato III MTT viability stayed ≥50% across all conditions, with moderate toxicity (~60% viability) in CA140 (and CA70 at 0.025 mg/mL, 24 h), while non-CA TOCNF and bPEI-TOCNF showed high compatibility.
ES_vs_SD_Comparative_Findings: No electrospinning arm; compared spray drying across TOCNF oxidation degrees and bPEI/CA crosslinker ratios, and contrasted SD microsponges against prior freeze-dried/thermally cured TOCNF aerogels (showing SD yields water-redispersible powders without hornification or salt addition and achieves single-step in situ amide crosslinking).
Limitations_and_Research_Gaps: High SD inlet temperature (210 °C; outlet 110–120 °C) precludes pre-loading of thermolabile drugs during spraying; TC loading capacity was modest (7%) and loading/release were conducted at room temperature rather than 37 °C; high CA crosslinking (CA140) lowered Kato III viability to ~60% due to positive surface charge and high swelling/medium interaction; no antimicrobial or in vivo assays were performed.
Research_Project_Takeaway: Demonstrates single-step spray drying of high-charge TOCNF (1.5 mmol COOH/g) with bPEI into non-hornifying, covalently amide-crosslinked microsponges (2–4 μm) capable of 70% tetracycline loading and pH-responsive gastric/topical release.

Titlu: “All oat!” Optimizing the spray drying process for oat oil emulsions stabilized by cellulose nanocrystals and methylcellulose
Autori: Megan G. Roberts, Keanna Yu, Marcus A. Johns, Golshan Matinfar, Emily D. Cranston
Dosage_Form_and_Route: Redispersible oil-filled microencapsulated powder (nutraceutical, cosmetic, and pharmaceutical applications)
Technology_Role: Spray drying of cellulose nanocrystal (CNC)-stabilized Pickering O/W emulsions into high-oil-loading, surfactant-free redispersible powders with 5-factor DOE optimization and oat-hull CNC biomass circularity
API_or_Cargo: Oat oil (Avena sativa): cold-pressed oat oil (Nature in Bottle) and ethanol-extracted oat oil (Mystic Moments)
Polymers_and_Carriers: Sulfated cellulose nanocrystals in sodium salt form (CelluForce CNCs, 128 x 8 nm by AFM, 203 ± 6 mmol/kg surface charge; and lab-isolated oat-hull CNCs, 220 ± 70 nm x 80 ± 20 nm by AFM, 78 ± 4 mmol/kg sulfate half-ester content) and food-grade methylcellulose (MC, Mw = 41,000 g/mol, DS 1.5-1.9, 400 cP)
Solvents_and_Additives: Purified MilliQ water (18.2 MΩ·cm), tannic acid (TA, polyphenol crosslinker), NaCl, phosphate buffer (Na2HPO4 and NaH2PO4·2H2O, pH 5.16); for oat-hull CNC isolation: NaOH, HCl, acetone, H2O2 (24 wt%), H2SO4 (64 wt%)
Formulation_Composition: Centre-point emulsion (45 mL total, 2:13 v/v oat oil:aqueous phase): 5.6 g oat oil, 6.6 g of 2.5 wt% CNC suspension, 7.95 g of 1.51 wt% MC solution, 1.2 g of 1 M NaCl, 8.65 g of 69 mM phosphate buffer (pH 5.16), and 15 mL of 0.8 wt% TA aqueous solution. Final pre-dilution aqueous concentrations: 0.42 wt% CNCs, 0.31 wt% MC, 0.31 wt% TA, 31 mM NaCl, 12 mM phosphate buffer (0.03 g CNC, 0.02 g MC, and 0.02 g TA per g oat oil; 0.07 g total stabilizer/g oat oil). In DOE, CNC varied at 0.0825 g (0.015 g/g oil), 0.165 g (0.030 g/g oil), and 0.330 g (0.059-0.06 g/g oil, 0.84 wt% pre-dilution), while MC and TA remained fixed at 0.02 g each/g oil; 30 mL emulsion samples were diluted 2x, 4x, or 8x with 50 mM NaCl / 20 mM phosphate buffer (pH 5.16).
Electrospinning_Setup_and_Params: N/A (spray-drying only study)
Spray_Drying_Setup_and_Params: Büchi B-290 Mini Spray Dryer (Switzerland); compressed air spray gas flow: 414 L/h; inlet temperature: 130-160 °C (centre 145 °C); outlet temperature: Not reported in source; pump rate: 4-12% (centre 8%), corresponding to liquid feed rate 1.4-4.0 mL/min (centre 2.1 mL/min); aspirator rate: 76-100% (centre 88%); liquid feed volume: 60-240 mL depending on dilution; drying time: 15-170 min; feed stirred magnetically throughout drying; nozzle diameter: Not reported in source.
Pre_and_Post_Processing: Pre-treatment: MC dissolved in purified water at 60-70 °C for 4 h then 4 °C overnight; pre-emulsion stirred (500 then 1200 rpm) and probe sonicated (Branson Sonifier 450, 15 mL batches, 60 s, 50% pulses, 60% output, ice bath), followed by TA addition, 20 min stirring, and second probe sonication (same settings). Oat-hull CNC isolation: blending, 250 μm sieving, alkali treatment (1.75 M NaOH, 70 °C, 2 h), HCl neutralization, centrifugation (5000 rpm, 15 min) + 2 acetone oil-extraction washes, 80 °C overnight drying, peroxide bleaching (5 wt% NaOH + 24 wt% H2O2, 70 °C, 1 h), 64 wt% H2SO4 hydrolysis (45 °C, 45 min), 10x ice-water quenching, centrifugation (6000 rpm, 10 min), and dialysis (14,000 Da MWCO until pH 5.5). Post-processing: collected powders stored at 4 °C; redispersion by adding 0.25 g powder to 10 mL purified water with 3 cycles of 10 s hand shaking + 10 s vortex mixing.
Characterization_Methods: AFM; TGA; Particle Size (Laser Diffraction / DLS); Zeta Potential; Electrical Conductivity / Surface Tension; Karl Fischer / Moisture Content
Characterization_Details: AFM measured commercial CelluForce CNCs at 128 x 8 nm and oat-hull CNCs at 220 ± 70 nm length x 80 ± 20 nm cross-section. Conductometric titration gave surface charges of 203 ± 6 mmol/kg (CelluForce CNCs) and 78 ± 4 mmol/kg sulfate half-ester content (oat-hull CNCs); DLS and zeta potential (Zetasizer Nano-ZS) of oat-hull CNCs gave 111 nm apparent hydrodynamic diameter and -27.7 mV. Laser diffraction and optical microscopy of the centre-point CNC-MC-TA cold-pressed oat oil emulsion showed 5.5 μm droplet diameter (span 1.7 μm; 5 ± 2 μm by optical microscopy) stable over 21 days at 4 °C without significant change in D[3,2] or D[4,3]; MC-only emulsions leaked oil over 3 weeks, and ethanol-extracted oat oil emulsions leaked overnight. TGA/DTG showed ethanol-extracted oil had a broader DTG peak; TGA/DTG of spray-dried powder separated stabilizer degradation (~290 °C) from oat oil (~410 °C). Redispersed powders reformed individual oil droplets without significant coalescence by laser diffraction and optical microscopy.
Performance_and_Bio_Assays: Encapsulation Efficiency / Process Yield; Physical / Chemical Stability (ICH / Accelerated)
Performance_Assay_Details: Spray-drying powder yield (Eq. S2) quantified across 19 DOE runs (16 half-factorial + 3 centre-point replicates) and modeled via multiple linear least-squares regression in IBM SPSS; powder oil content determined by integrating TGA/DTG peaks (~290 °C stabilizers vs ~410 °C oat oil); encapsulation confirmed by aqueous redispersion (0.25 g in 10 mL water, 3x 10 s hand shake + 10 s vortex) with laser diffraction and optical microscopy. Emulsion physical stability monitored over 21 days at 4 °C; lipid hydroperoxides in cold-pressed vs ethanol-extracted oat oils quantified via ferrous oxidation-xylenol orange (FOX) assay.
Key_Quantitative_Results: Centre-point emulsion droplet size: 5.5 μm (span 1.7 μm; 5 ± 2 μm microscopy), stable 21 days; centre-point spray-drying yield: ~55% (DOE range 9.4-82%, average 50%, 5 runs >=60%); optimal DOE run (Sample 15: 0.330 g CNC [0.06 g/g oil], 8x dilution, 100% aspirator, 4% pump, 160 °C) reached 82% yield; powder oil content: 89.1% (vs 90.8% theoretical maximum); moisture content: <2%; DOE yield model (R2 = 0.80, Q2 = 0.59, p = 0.00034): Y = -64.15 + 231.2x1 + 3.421x2 + 0.5039x3 + 4.161x4 - 16.42x1x4 (contributions: CNC 48, aspirator 44, pump 33, dilution 17, CNC x pump -35). Oat-hull CNC recovery yield: 5% bleached solids (10 g/200 g hulls), 0.25% purified CNCs (0.5 g); 'All Oat!' centre-point spray-drying yield: 47% (1.9 g powder).
ES_vs_SD_Comparative_Findings: No electrospinning performed; compares spray drying against freeze drying and spray-freeze drying from prior group work (Massicotte & Cranston, 2022), concluding spray drying is faster, lower-energy, and gives the smallest redispersed droplet size by avoiding freezing-induced aggregation. Also achieves 89.1% oil loading at 0.07 g total stabilizer/g oil (~10-20x lower stabilizer than literature CNC-only [1.1-1.4 g/g] or CNC/HPMC [0.8 g/g] spray-dried oil powders).
Limitations_and_Research_Gaps: Three low-CNC DOE trials (samples 4, 6, 8) formed tacky, brownish, liquid-like products; inlet temperature was restricted to 130-160 °C (<130 °C gave wet/gum-like products with oil leakage; >160 °C caused discolouration and burnt-oat odor for runs >1.5 h); 8x dilution extended drying up to 2 h 50 min; DOE model was not predictive for moisture content or redispersed droplet size; oat-hull CNC recovery was very low (0.25%) with lower aspect ratio and charge (78 mmol/kg) leading to more droplet agglomeration; no long-term powder oxidative/shelf-life stability, in vitro release/bioaccessibility, or in vivo PK/efficacy assays were performed.
Research_Project_Takeaway: This study provides the first 5-factor DOE optimization of spray-dried CNC-MC-TA Pickering emulsions, achieving 82% yield, 89.1% oat oil loading, and <2% moisture with only 0.06 g CNC/g oil. Demonstrating an 'All Oat!' circular system using oat-hull CNCs confirms the feasibility of surfactant-free, biomass-derived nanocellulose carriers for oxidation-sensitive nutraceutical and pharmaceutical oils.

Characterization_Methods: SEM; Particle Size (Laser Diffraction / DLS); Zeta Potential; Powder Flow / Bulk-Tapped Density; Karl Fischer / Moisture Content; Micro-CT / Confocal Microscopy
Characterization_Details: Emulsion droplet size D(3,2) by laser diffraction (Malvern Mastersizer 2000) and optical microscopy (Shunyu CX40, 20×); dry microcapsule size by Mastersizer 2000 with Scirocco 2000 dry autosampler; SEM (Hitachi S4800, 10 kV, 1000×, Au-coated); zeta potential (Malvern Zetasizer Nano ZS at 0.1% m/m in distilled water); angle of repose (5 mL powder funnel method) and bulk density (graduated cylinder); moisture content (oven drying of 0.5 g sample); z-stack CLSM (Olympus FV3000, Nile red 573–591 nm for VE oil and FITC 498–517 nm for gelatin).
Performance_and_Bio_Assays: Encapsulation Efficiency / Process Yield; HPLC / UV-Vis / Assay & Content Uniformity; Physical / Chemical Stability (ICH / Accelerated)
Performance_Assay_Details: UV-Vis quantification (Shimadzu UV-1750, 285 nm, R2 = 0.9978) of total VE (20 min pulsed sonication extraction in absolute ethanol at 20 kHz, 50% amplitude) and surface VE (3 × 10 mL petroleum ether washes, rotary evaporation, ethanol redissolution) to determine microencapsulation yield (MEY), microencapsulation efficiency (MEE), VE loading rate, and surface oil content; 10-day visual storage physical stability (creaming/stratification) of feed emulsions.
Key_Quantitative_Results: Increasing gelatin from 3% to 7% reduced emulsion D(3,2) from 7.8 to 3.9 μm (6% gelatin gave unimodal droplets and was fixed). Emulsions without BCNFs exhibited multimodal size and creaming over 10 days, whereas 0.2–0.4% BCNFs prevented stratification. Microcapsules ranged 1–150 μm (main fraction 10–50 μm), with mean powder size decreasing from 28.6 to 13.5 μm as BCNFs rose from 0.2% to 0.4%; zeta potential was ~ -20 mV. Across 0%, 0.2%, 0.3%, and 0.4% BCNFs: moisture content was 2.98 ± 0.18%, 3.02 ± 0.17%, 3.21 ± 0.23%, and 3.28 ± 0.10%; angle of repose improved from 60.0 ± 2.1° (0%) to 45.2 ± 1.3° (0.2%), 46.6 ± 1.2° (0.3%), and 44.6 ± 1.2° (0.4%); bulk density dropped from 0.191 ± 0.016 g/cm3 (0%) to 0.174 ± 0.002, 0.169 ± 0.006, and 0.171 ± 0.002 g/cm3; MEY was 68.70 ± 0.42%, 81.80 ± 0.74% (peak at 0.2% BCNFs), 73.30 ± 0.43%, and 73.00 ± 0.43%; MEE was 56.80 ± 0.44%, 62.90 ± 1.08% (peak), 60.00 ± 0.89%, and 58.40 ± 0.45%; VE loading rate was 39.22%, 46.51% (peak), 41.59%, and 41.34%; surface oil content decreased from 43.2% (0%) to 37.1% (0.2% BCNFs), 40.0% (0.3%), and 41.6% (0.4%). At 0.4% BCNFs, SEM showed high powder agglomeration.
ES_vs_SD_Comparative_Findings: No electrospinning arm; compared BCNFs-stabilized Pickering emulsion spray drying (0.2–0.4% BCNFs) against BCNFs-free gelatin/maltodextrin/PVP emulsion spray drying, showing 0.2% BCNFs maximized MEY (81.8%), MEE (62.9%), and VE loading (46.51%) while reducing surface oil (37.1%) and repose angle (45.2°).
Limitations_and_Research_Gaps: Surface oil remained relatively high (37.1% at optimal 0.2% BCNFs) and MEE was 62.90%; ≥0.4% BCNFs induced powder agglomeration and reduced yield/efficiency; no dry-powder oxidative/UV storage stability, no in vitro drug/vitamin release or digestion testing, and no FTIR/DSC/XRD solid-state characterization were reported.
Research_Project_Takeaway: Shows that incorporating 0.2% (m/m) bacterial cellulose nanofibrils with 6% gelatin in O/W Pickering emulsions prior to spray drying suppresses droplet collapse, boosts Vitamin E loading to 46.51% (MEY 81.8%), and lowers surface oil and angle of repose.

Autori: Maria‐Beatrice Coltelli, Pierfrancesco Morganti, Valter Castelvetro, Andrea Lazzeri, Serena Danti et al.
Dosage_Form_and_Route: Topical / skin-contact spray-dried nanostructured powders and surface-modifying micro-platelets (for cosmetics, sanitary pads, protective items, wound dressings, and polymer extrusion coatings)
Technology_Role: Spray drying of electrostatically complexed chitin nanofibril–nanolignin (CN-NL) gels with 2 wt% PEG as an anti-agglomerating agent to prevent irreversible nanofibril bundling and generate redispersible porous microparticles / flat surface-adhering micro-platelets carrying functional actives.
API_or_Cargo: Vitamin E (alpha-tocopherol, VE), sodium ascorbyl phosphate (vitamin C derivative, VC), lutein (LU), nicotinamide (NI), glycyrrhetinic acid (GA), and silver nanoparticles (AG, 0.1 wt%, avg. 61.9 nm)
Polymers_and_Carriers: Shrimp-sourced chitin nanofibrils (CNs), Biolignin nanolignin (NL, Mw 980 g/mol, 91% lignin content), and poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG, Mw 8000)
Solvents_and_Additives: Slightly acidic water (for electrostatic CN-NL complexation/gelation) and 2 wt% PEG 8000 (anti-agglomerating agent during spray drying)
Formulation_Composition: CN:NL weight ratio 2:1; PEG added at 2 wt% to inhibit electrostatic aggregation; active molecules (VE, VC, LU, NI, GA) encapsulated at 0.2% to 5% based on chitin weight (exact per-formulation loadings from Table 1 are not in the extracted PMC text); Ag nanoparticles added at 0.1 wt% in CN/AG and CN-NL/AG.
Electrospinning_Setup_and_Params: Not applicable (spray drying of preformed chitin nanofibrils).
Spray_Drying_Setup_and_Params: Büchi Mini Spray Dryer B-190 (Flawil, Switzerland) processing aqueous CN-PEG and CN-NL/M-PEG gels containing 2 wt% PEG 8000; exact inlet/outlet temperatures, feed rate, and nozzle size were not reported in the extracted text (cited to prior methods/patents).
Pre_and_Post_Processing: Pre-SD: Electrostatic gelation of positively charged CN in slightly acidic water with active molecules and negatively charged NL (2:1 CN:NL). Post-SD: Aqueous redispersion (e.g., 1:1000 v/v) for surface deposition (forming flat ellipsoidal micro-platelets) or solubilization in physiological saline (pH ~7) for HaCaT assays; evaluated for downstream high-temperature polymer melt blending/extrusion coating.
Characterization_Details: FESEM (FEI FEG-Quanta 450, Au-sputtered, imaging dry powders and 1:1000 aqueous dispersions dried on glass); ATR-FTIR (Nicolet T380 with Smart ITX diamond plate, 4000–550 cm-1, 4 cm-1 resolution, 256 scans); TGA/SDTA (Mettler-Toledo 851, 4–10 mg, 25–800 °C at 10 °C/min, N2 60 mL/min); BET surface area of dried CN powder (Micromeritics Gemini V).
Performance_and_Bio_Assays: Cytotoxicity / Hemolysis / Biocompatibility
Performance_Assay_Details: HaCaT human keratinocyte viability by MTT assay (0.5 mg/mL MTT, 570–655 nm) after 48 h across 1:10 to 1:4000 saline dilutions (and 24 h MTT from 10 μg/mL to 25 ng/mL for CN, CN-NL, CN-NL/GA); real-time PCR (Roche LightCycler, SYBR Green, β-actin housekeeping control) on HaCaT cells (treated with 10 μg/mL CN, 0.2 μg/mL CN-NL, or 0.5 μg/mL CN-NL/M for 6 h and 24 h) measuring IL-1α, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, TNF-α, TGF-β, and antimicrobial peptide human β-defensin-2 (HBD-2).
Key_Quantitative_Results: Conventionally dried CN formed aggregated bundles with BET surface area of 1.7–3.4 m2/g, whereas spray-drying CN with 2 wt% PEG produced porous round microparticles stable in water; spray-dried CN-NL-PEG formed round microparticles that deposited from water as smooth flat ellipsoidal micro-platelets. All powders were thermally stable below 140 °C (<5% mass loss up to 200 °C; main degradation peak ~300 °C with 60–70% weight loss in 200–350 °C for complexes vs. ~20% for pure CN). Pure active/control 5% mass-loss temperatures (5%ML): VC (70 °C) < NI (140 °C) < VE = LU (180 °C) < GA = CN/AG (240 °C); GA, LU, and VE slightly improved CN-NL thermal stability, while Ag yielded higher residue (12.01% for CN/AG vs. 4.41% for CN-NL/AG). In HaCaT MTT assays, CN-NL/AG required ≥1:4000 dilution (showing only 62.5 ± 5% viability even at 1:4000), and CN-NL/VE and CN-NL/LU required ≥1:2000 dilution, whereas >100% cell viability was observed for CN (1:10), CN-NL/GA (1:200), CN-NL (1:500), and CN-NL/VC (1:500). At 6 h, complexes upregulated IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-1α, downregulated IL-8, and all except CN-NL/GA induced HBD-2 expression; all cytokines returned to or below baseline by 24 h. CN and CN-NL/GA offered the best combination of thermal stability and keratinocyte cytocompatibility.
ES_vs_SD_Comparative_Findings: No electrospinning arm; contrasted spray-dried CN-PEG and CN-NL/M-PEG complexes against conventionally dried CN powders and Ag-loaded controls, showing spray drying with 2 wt% PEG suppresses fibril aggregation into low-surface-area bundles and generates porous microparticles / surface-coating ellipsoidal micro-platelets.
Limitations_and_Research_Gaps: Exact Büchi B-190 spray-drying parameters (temperatures, feed rate, nozzle), particle size distributions, encapsulation efficiency, and active release profiles were not reported in the paper; antimicrobial activity was inferred only from keratinocyte HBD-2 mRNA expression without bacterial MIC/killing assays; numerical Tables 1–6 were omitted from the extracted PMC XML text.
Research_Project_Takeaway: Provides a systematic thermal-stability and HaCaT-cytocompatibility screening matrix for spray-dried chitin nanofibril–nanolignin (2:1) + 2 wt% PEG complexes carrying skin bioactives, highlighting CN and CN-NL/glycyrrhetinic acid for thermally processed skin-contact products.

Dosage_Form_and_Route: Spray-dried nanocomposite microparticles (multiparticulate raw material for oral tablets or capsules); oral colon-specific delivery
Technology_Role: Spray drying produces spherical 1-10 µm retrograded starch/pectin (RS/P) microparticles from aqueous dispersions, while pre-formed cellulose nanofibers (CNF) act as nanoreinforcement to suppress premature burst release in gastric and duodenal fluids and target 5-ASA to the colon.

Formulation_Composition: Retrogradation study: HAS (5% m/v) + P (5% m/v) + CNF (3.8% m/v) at HAS:P:CNF ratios of 1:1:0, 1:1:0.25, 1:1:0.50, 1:1:0.75, 1:1:1 or HAS:CNF 1:0.25, 1:0.5, 1:0.75, 1:1. XRD (Siemens D5000, Cu-Kα 1.5406 Å, 3-90° 2θ, 0.05°/s): CNF peaks at 16.2° and 22.5°; HAS B-type peaks (15°, 17.1°, 19.9°, 22.5°, 24°); RS V-type peak at 13°; in situ CNF increased 22.5° intensity and reduced RS crystallinity. TG-DSC (Mettler Toledo TG/DSC 1, N2 50 mL/min, 10 °C/min) and DSC (TA Instruments Q10): pectin improved thermal stability of RS/CNF; RS/P 1:1 showed lowest moisture mass loss (30-150 °C). Bulk/tapped density (2 g in 10 mL cylinder), Hausner ratio (1.81-2.50), and Carr's index (45-60%) showed cohesive, poor flow.
Performance_and_Bio_Assays: In Vitro Dissolution / Drug Release; HPLC / UV-Vis / Assay & Content Uniformity; Encapsulation Efficiency / Process Yield

Process yield measured gravimetrically (n=3). EE% and DL determined by dispersing 30 mg microparticles in 3 mL 0.1 M pH 7.4 phosphate buffer (48 h stirring, centrifugation 5000 rpm 10 min, 0.45 µm nylon filtration, UV-Vis Hewlett Packard 8452 at 331 nm, r2=0.9999). In vitro 5-ASA release (10 mg 5-ASA equivalent, n=3) performed in Hanson SR-8Plus modified USP type I mini-basket with 14,000 Da dialysis bag (150 mL, 50 rpm, 37 °C) sequentially in SGF (0.1 N HCl, pH 1.2, 1 h), SDF (0.1 M acetate buffer, pH 4.5, 1 h), and SCF (0.1 M phosphate buffer, pH 6.8, 5 h), quantified by UV-Vis at 303, 302, and 331 nm; kinetics fitted via Sigma Plot 10.
Key_Quantitative_Results: RS content ranged 32.35-73% (highest 73% for RS/P without CNF; in situ CNF impaired retrogradation). Optimized spray drying (210 °C, 70% aspirator, 0.05% pump flow) gave 57% yield (reducing pump flow from 0.15% to 0.05% improved yield by 57.1%) and 1.2% moisture. Across formulations, EE% ranged 16-98% and DL 1.97-26.63%: RS/P/5ASA without surfactant achieved EE% > 90%, while polysorbate 80 dropped EE% to 47%. RS/P/5ASA-CNF10 and CNF25 reached ~95% EE% and 13.2-14.7 mg/100 mg DL, whereas CNF50 dropped significantly due to high viscosity and nozzle clogging. Free 5-ASA dissolved 100% within 60 min in SGF; unreinforced RS/P/5ASA released ~25% in SGF and 68% in SDF. CNF10, CNF25, and CNF50 released ~12%, 15%, and 25% in SGF (60 min); in SDF (120 min), RS/P/5ASA-CNF25 was best (34% cumulative release), targeting 55-65% of the drug load to SCF. Release best fitted Weibull (CNF10/CNF50: 0.75 < b < 1, non-Fickian Case-II; CNF25: b < 0.75, Fickian diffusion via surface pores).
ES_vs_SD_Comparative_Findings: Not a head-to-head comparison; electrospinning is mentioned only briefly in the introduction alongside spray drying and electrospraying as colon-specific formulation technologies. The work integrates pre-formed CNF into spray-dried RS/P microparticles to mitigate the rapid upper-GIT release caused by spray-drying-induced amorphization and small particle size (<10 µm).
Limitations_and_Research_Gaps: 1) Adding CNF prior to starch retrogradation reduced RS yield (from 73% down to 32.35-68.3%), requiring CNF addition immediately before spray drying. 2) High CNF loading (50% m/m) elevated dispersion viscosity, caused nozzle clogging, flattened particles, and lowered EE% and DL. 3) All spray-dried powders exhibited poor flowability (Hausner ratio 1.81-2.50, Carr's index 45-60%), necessitating flow additives (e.g., magnesium stearate) or downstream tableting/encapsulation. 4) Gastric release (12-25% at 60 min) still exceeded the <10% at 2 h gastro-resistance criterion cited by the authors, and colonic microbiota enzymatic degradation was not incorporated into the pH-gradient dissolution test.
Research_Project_Takeaway: Shows that incorporating pre-formed cellulose nanofibers (25% m/m) immediately before spray drying reinforces amorphous retrograded starch/pectin microparticles, curbing duodenal 5-ASA release (34% vs 68% at 120 min) to target 55-65% of the dose to the colon, while identifying 50% CNF viscosity/clogging limits and poor spray-dried powder flowability.

Titlu: Dry Powder Inhalers for Proteins Using Cryo-Milled Electrospun Polyvinyl Alcohol Nanofiber Mats.
Autori: Takaaki Ito, Eriko Yamazoe, Kohei Tahara
Dosage_Form_and_Route: Dry powder inhaler (DPI) porous cryo-milled nanofiber particles loaded into No. 2 HPMC hard capsules; pulmonary inhalation
Technology_Role: Electrospinning prepares protein-loaded solid-dispersion PVA nanofiber mats without heating or high shear, and cryo-milling converts the mats into porous 5-30 µm low-density particles with respirable aerodynamic properties (MMAD 5.9 µm) as a heat-free alternative to spray drying and jet-milling for labile proteins.
API_or_Cargo: α-chymotrypsin (α-Chy, Sigma-Aldrich, 1% w/w of total solute = 3.2 mg per 4.0 mL); uranine (Tokyo Chemical Industry, 1% w/w = 3.2 mg, fluorescent label for ACI aerosol testing)
Polymers_and_Carriers: Polyvinyl alcohol (PVA, GOHSENOL EG-40P, degree of polymerization 2400, degree of hydrolysis 88 mol%, Mitsubishi Chemical Co., 99% w/w of total solute = 316.8 mg per 4.0 mL)
Solvents_and_Additives: Distilled water (solvent); No. 2 hydroxypropyl methylcellulose (HPMC) hard capsules (Qualicaps) for DPI testing
Formulation_Composition: Total solute concentration 320.0 mg in 4.0 mL distilled water (8% w/v), consisting of 1% w/w (3.2 mg) α-Chy or uranine and 99% w/w (316.8 mg) PVA.
Electrospinning_Setup_and_Params: 5 mL syringe with 22-gauge needle; syringe pump (Yutaka Electric Co.) at 0.5 mL/h; high-voltage power supply (MECC Co., Ltd.) at 10 kV; grounded aluminum-covered collector; tip-to-collector distance 10 cm; temperature 20-25 °C; relative humidity < 50%.
Spray_Drying_Setup_and_Params: Not experimentally performed (spray drying and jet-milling are discussed as conventional DPI manufacturing methods whose heating and shear stresses denature proteins and produce dense, cohesive single-micron particles requiring large lactose carriers).
Pre_and_Post_Processing: Pre-processing: PVA dissolved in distilled water at 80 °C with stirring and cooled to room temperature before adding α-Chy or uranine. Post-processing: ~50 mg of electrospun nanofiber mat placed in a 12 mL sample cell with two 15 mm steel balls in a cryo-mill (JFC-300, Japan Analytical Industry Co., Ltd.), immersed in liquid nitrogen for 5 or 30 min, and milled for 1, 3, or 5 min.
Characterization_Details: SEM (JEOL JSM-6510LV, 5 kV, platinum sputter-coated via JFC-1600): electrospun PVA nanofibers were 300-600 nm in diameter; cryo-milled mats frozen for 30 min and milled for 1 or 3 min formed 5-30 µm porous particles retaining fibrous morphology, whereas 5 min milling or 5 min freezing destroyed the fiber structure. Dry laser diffraction (MicrotracBEL LDSA-SPR 3500A, n=3): at 3 min milling, 5 vs 30 min freezing gave median geometric diameter D50 of 14.37 µm vs 12.60 µm; D50 decreased inversely with milling time down to 7.36 µm at 5 min milling (30 min freezing).
Performance_and_Bio_Assays: Aerodynamic Assessment (NGI / ACI / TSI); Probiotic / Cell / Biologic Viability (CFU / Activity); Physical / Chemical Stability (ICH / Accelerated); HPLC / UV-Vis / Assay & Content Uniformity
Performance_Assay_Details: In vitro aerosolization (n=3): 3 mg uranine-loaded milled mat in No. 2 HPMC capsules tested via Jethaler reverse-type DPI connected to an 8-stage Andersen cascade impactor (ACI AN-200, glycerin-coated stainless-steel plates, 28.3 L/min, 5 s, 8.7 kPa pressure drop); stage deposits rinsed with 10 mL PBS and quantified by fluorescence (GloMax-Multi, Ex 490 nm, Em 510-570 nm) for delivered dose (DD), fine particle fraction (FPF < 4.7 µm), and MMAD (Tukey's test). α-Chy enzymatic activity: 22.5 mg milled mat dissolved in 1.5 mL PBS (150 µg/mL α-Chy, 1 h), reacted with 20 µL 60 mM p-nitrophenyl acetate in DMSO for 30 min, and p-nitrophenol measured by UV-Vis (Shimadzu UV-1800, 404 nm). Long-term storage stability (n=3): ~25 mg milled mats (30 min freeze, 3 min mill) in fabric-covered glass vials stored in airtight silica-gel containers at 20-25 °C for 6 months vs freshly prepared mats and control aqueous α-Chy solution.
Key_Quantitative_Results: Optimal cryo-milling (30 min liquid-nitrogen freezing, 3 min milling) produced porous particles with geometric D50 = 12.60 µm, MMAD = 5.9 µm, maximum FPF (<4.7 µm) = 26.5% (20-fold higher than 5 min freezing / 3 min milling, p < 0.01), and DD > 75% across all groups. Electrospinning caused ~12% loss in α-Chy activity compared to untreated α-Chy solution. All milled mats frozen for 30 min retained >80% enzymatic activity relative to unmilled nanofiber mats (n=1 for milling comparison), whereas 5 min freezing / 3 min milling dropped activity to 68.6%. After 6 months at 20-25 °C with silica gel, 30 min freeze / 3 min milled mats retained 96.4% of initial mat activity (n=3), whereas the control α-Chy solution lost 36.0% activity.
ES_vs_SD_Comparative_Findings: Spray drying and jet-milling are compared conceptually (not tested experimentally): they expose biologics to heat and shear stresses causing denaturation and yield dense single-micron particles with high interparticle adhesion requiring 50-100 µm lactose carrier blending. Electrospinning + cryo-milling eliminates heating, creates low-density porous 5-30 µm particles (D50 12.6 µm) achieving a respirable MMAD of 5.9 µm without lactose carriers, and preserves protein activity over 6 months.
Limitations_and_Research_Gaps: 1) Electrospinning itself reduced α-Chy activity by ~12% and milling caused additional time-dependent loss (authors suggest core-shell electrospinning or voltage/shear optimization). 2) ACI aerosol performance was measured using uranine-labeled mats rather than direct α-Chy quantification, and full D10/D90/Span and per-condition DD/FPF/MMAD table values are absent from the extracted text. 3) Low drug loading (1% w/w) and small batch cryo-milling scale (~50 mg/cell) leave industrial scalability and design space unestablished.
Research_Project_Takeaway: Demonstrates a heat-free electrospinning + cryo-milling workflow (30 min N2 freeze, 3 min mill) that converts PVA protein nanofiber mats into carrier-free porous DPI powders (D50 12.6 µm, MMAD 5.9 µm, FPF 26.5%, DD > 75%) while retaining >80% post-milling α-chymotrypsin activity and 96.4% stability over 6 months.

Titlu: Preformulation Studies of Furosemide-Loaded Electrospun Nanofibrous Systems for Buccal Administration.
Autori: Andrea Kovács, Balázs Démuth, Andrea Meskó, Romána Zelkó
Dosage_Form_and_Route: Electrospun mucoadhesive nanofibrous mats (preformulation for transmucosal buccal administration)
Technology_Role: Aqueous electrospinning converts crystalline BCS IV furosemide into an amorphous solid dispersion within mucoadhesive HPC/PVP nanofibers; polymer ratio dictates gel viscoelasticity (G''/G') and drives a morphological transition from uniform nanofibers (HPC:PVP 6:4) to mixed fibers/droplets and predominantly electrosprayed droplets (referred to by the authors as 'spray-dried droplets') at 9:1.
API_or_Cargo: Furosemide (Ph. Eur., BCS class IV poorly soluble/permeable loop diuretic; 0.2 g per batch)
Polymers_and_Carriers: Hydroxypropyl cellulose (HPC, Klucel EXF Pharm, Ashland, Mw ~80,000, MS = 3.8, mucoadhesive polymer); Poly(vinylpyrrolidone) (PVP, Kollidon 90 F, BASF, Mw ~1,000,000-1,500,000, electrospinnability-enhancing polymer)
Solvents_and_Additives: Purified water (17.2 g per batch, aqueous solvent); Trolamine (Ph. Eur., Molar Chemicals, 0.3 g per batch, solubilizer and intended buccal penetration enhancer)
Formulation_Composition: Furosemide stock solution: 0.2 g furosemide + 0.3 g trolamine in 17.2 g purified water. Total polymer concentration fixed at 15 wt% across 5 HPC:PVP ratios: 5:5, 6:4, 7:3, 8:2, and 9:1 (described as w/w in Methods/Fig. 2 and as molar ratio in Fig. 3-5 captions).
Electrospinning_Setup_and_Params: Syringes connected via silicone tubes to needles (internal diameter 1.2 mm [stated as '1.2']); applied voltage 25 kV; needle-to-collector distance 15 cm; flow rate 0.3 mL/h; aluminum foil collector; room temperature (25 °C).
Spray_Drying_Setup_and_Params: Not applicable (no spray dryer was used; the 'spray-dried droplets' described in the abstract and Section 3.3 are electrosprayed droplets produced during electrospinning of high-HPC compositions, explicitly called 'electrosprayed structure' in Section 3.4).
Pre_and_Post_Processing: Pre-processing: furosemide dissolved in purified water with trolamine under magnetic stirring in a dark beaker, followed by PVP mixing at 25 °C until homogeneous and portion-wise HPC addition at 25 °C. Physical mixtures prepared by 5 min mortar mixing for FTIR. Fibers/droplets dried at room temperature during electrospinning; no post-processing required.
Characterization_Details: Oscillatory rheology (Malvern Kinexus Pro, 50 mm parallel plates, 0.0300 mm gap, 25 ± 0.1 °C, 30% amplitude in LVR, 0.1-10 s^-1, G''/G' plotted at 1.995 Hz): HPC:PVP 6:4 was the most elastic gel (lowest G''/G') and yielded the most homogeneous fibrous mat. SEM (JEOL 6380LVa, 15 kV, 10 mm WD, gold-sputtered, ImageJ n=50): 5:5 and 6:4 formed predominantly nanofibers; 7:3 and 8:2 formed mixed nanofibers and droplets; 9:1 formed almost totally electrosprayed droplets. ATR-FTIR (Jasco FT/IR-4200, ATR PRO470-H, 100 scans): crystalline furosemide sulfonamide NH (3397, 3281 cm^-1) and secondary amine NH (3349 cm^-1) bands present in raw drug and 6:4 physical mixture vanished in 6:4 nanofibers, while PVP (1653 cm^-1) and HPC (1100 cm^-1) bands remained, confirming amorphous solid dispersion.
Performance_and_Bio_Assays: None performed / Not reported in source
Performance_Assay_Details: None performed (preformulation study limited to gel rheology, SEM morphology/fiber diameter statistics, and ATR-FTIR solid-state characterization; no dissolution, drug assay, mucoadhesion, or buccal permeation tests were performed).
Key_Quantitative_Results: At 15 wt% total polymer, mean fiber diameters (n=50) were 618.76 ± 193.617 nm (HPC:PVP 5:5), 443.89 ± 158.376 nm (6:4), 419.43 ± 116.048 nm (7:3), and 367.50 ± 153.908 nm (8:2), while 9:1 yielded almost exclusively electrosprayed droplets. Kolmogorov-Smirnov confirmed normal distributions (p = 0.964, 0.992, 0.641, 0.410); ANOVA showed significant diameter differences (p < 0.001; 5:5 was significantly thicker than 6:4, 7:3, and 8:2). HPC:PVP 6:4 exhibited optimal viscoelasticity (lowest G''/G' at 1.995 Hz) and highest fiber homogeneity. ATR-FTIR confirmed disappearance of crystalline furosemide NH peaks (3397, 3349, 3281 cm^-1) in 6:4 fibers.
ES_vs_SD_Comparative_Findings: No actual spray drying was performed. The study documents a polymer-ratio-dependent transition during aqueous electrospinning from homogeneous nanofibers (HPC:PVP 6:4) to mixed fibers/droplets (7:3, 8:2) and predominantly electrosprayed droplets (9:1), which the authors informally term 'spray-dried droplets'.
Limitations_and_Research_Gaps: 1) Purely preformulation: lacks in vitro drug release/dissolution, drug loading/content uniformity, mucoadhesion force, stability, and ex vivo buccal permeation assays needed to substantiate improved oral/buccal bioavailability. 2) Solid-state amorphization relied solely on ATR-FTIR without XRD or DSC confirmation. 3) Minor reporting inconsistencies exist (w/w vs molar ratio labels for HPC:PVP across text vs figure captions; 4000-1800 cm^-1 scan range stated in Methods vs 1600-500 cm^-1 bands discussed in Results).
Research_Project_Takeaway: Not a true spray-drying study ('spray-dried droplets' refers to electrosprayed droplets at high HPC:PVP ratios), but establishes aqueous electrospinning preformulation rules linking HPC:PVP gel viscoelasticity (G''/G') to fiber-vs-droplet morphology and amorphous furosemide incorporation at 15 wt% HPC:PVP 6:4.

Thermal resistance / survival assay: free L. plantarum, PVA+probiotic nanofibers, and CA/PVA+probiotic/CA sandwich nanofibers (standardized to 10^7 CFU/mL in 40 mL yogurt soda [dough] test media) were heat-treated at 75 °C for 0, 1, 3, 5, and 8 min, with 1 mL aliquots enumerated via serial dilution and MRS agar plating.
Key_Quantitative_Results: PVA nanofiber diameters: 90-500 nm. Encapsulation efficiency: 89.8% for trilayer CA/PVA+probiotic/CA sandwich nanofibers (130,103 unencapsulated CFU/mL from 1,277,818 CFU/mL initial) vs 81.0% for single-layer PVA+probiotic nanofibers (247,716 unencapsulated CFU/mL from 1,277,818 CFU/mL initial), representing an 8.8 percentage-point (~9%) improvement. Heat stability at 75 °C in yogurt soda: free probiotics were completely inactivated within 5 min, whereas trilayer CA/PVA+probiotic/CA nanofibers preserved viable bacteria for up to 8 min. TGA confirmed complete degradation of PVA+probiotic at 500-530 °C while CA outer layers slowed thermal weight loss.
ES_vs_SD_Comparative_Findings: Spray drying was not performed experimentally, but cited as a conventional method prone to heat-induced bacterial loss (referencing 3-4 min high-temperature survival in prior spray-dried probiotic microcapsules and 60-75% GI survival for whey protein-alginate systems), whereas trilayer CA/PVA/CA electrospinning reached 89.8% EE and 8 min survival at 75 °C.
Limitations_and_Research_Gaps: 1) Although the title and abstract reference acidic/GI conditions, no dedicated experimental SGF (pH 1.5-3.5) or bile-salt survival assay is described in Methods/Results—only heat treatment at 75 °C in yogurt soda (dough) was performed. 2) Long-term shelf-life storage stability and release kinetics in intestinal pH were not tested. 3) Acetone/DMF solvents for the CA layers raise residual solvent toxicity concerns for food/pharma use and were not quantified. 4) Several reporting inconsistencies/errors appear in the paper (acetone/DMF ratio 1:2 in 2.2 vs 2:1 in 3.1; electrospinning params 20 kV/1 mL/h/15 cm in 2.4 vs 22 kV/1.3 mL/h/14 cm in 3.1; '13500 cm^-1' FTIR typo; malformed Table 1 column layout; SD values omitted in Table 1). 5) Pilot-scale throughput of sequential 3-layer electrospinning remains unverified.
Research_Project_Takeaway: Shows that a sequentially electrospun trilayer CA/PVA+probiotic/CA sandwich mat boosts L. plantarum NIMBB003 encapsulation efficiency to 89.8% (vs 81% for single-layer PVA) and extends 75 °C thermal survival from <5 min to 8 min as a non-thermal alternative to spray drying, though residual acetone/DMF and missing SGF/storage tests remain gaps.

Polymers_and_Carriers: Polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP K-90, Mw 360,000, Sigma-Aldrich).
Solvents_and_Additives: Milli-Q water; 0.1 M phosphate buffer pH 7.4 containing 0.15 M NaCl (PBS, required to preserve VLP structural integrity).
Formulation_Composition: 30% w/v PVP K-90 in Milli-Q water mixed at a 1:1 ratio with 5 mg purified VLP dialyzed against PBS (final 15% w/v PVP in PBS), magnetically stirred for 20 min.
Electrospinning_Setup_and_Params: 5-mL syringe (Becton Dickinson) with blunted 18 G needle; Chemyx Fusion Touch 100 infusion pump at 0.1 mL/h; 24 kV applied voltage; 15 cm tip-to-collector distance; grounded rotating metal wheel collector (~10 rpm) wrapped with aluminum foil; ambient temperature and atmospheric pressure.
Spray_Drying_Setup_and_Params: Not experimentally performed (discussed as a comparator literature process noting nebulization shear stress and heated dehydration stress requiring multi-component excipient systems, e.g., Saboo et al. for HPV VLPs).
Pre_and_Post_Processing: VLP expressed in Sf21 insect cells (flashBAC Ultra baculovirus, MOI 1, 27 °C, 125 rpm, 3 days), lysed with 0.5% Triton X-100, purified by differential centrifugation and 1.2/1.4 g/mL CsCl step gradient (100,000 g, 18 h), and dialyzed into PBS. Electrospun mats stored on aluminum foil in zip-locked bags with silica gel at room temperature for up to 7 days; dissolved in PBS (with 25 ug CpG 1826 added post-dissolution for in vivo vaccination) or re-purified on CsCl gradient for TEM recovery checks.
Characterization_Details: SEM (Carl Zeiss variable-pressure SEM; 5 nmol Au-Pd sputter coat via Emitech K575X) showed heterogeneous tubular strands and flat ribbon-like sheets (100 nm to 5 um diameter) with singular and clustered VLP-sized particles on the surface of loaded mats. TEM (Philips CM100, 1% phosphotungstic acid pH 6.8) confirmed ~40 nm icosahedral VLPs before spinning and after mat dissolution plus CsCl re-purification. 10% SDS-PAGE (60 kDa VP60 band), mass spectrometry (gp100 sequence), and fluorescent anti-VP60 Western blot (LI-COR Odyssey FC at 800 nm, 0.1 cm2 mat sections vs 0.0625-4 ug standards) confirmed VP60 identity and uniform loading across the mat.
Performance_and_Bio_Assays: Probiotic / Cell / Biologic Viability (CFU / Activity); In Vivo PK / Efficacy
Performance_Assay_Details: In vitro co-culture of C57BL/6 BMDCs (5 x 10^4 cells/mL, pulsed directly with nanofiber sections containing 1 ug VLP, PBS VLP, or molar-equivalent gp100 peptide at 0.38 ug/mL) and CFSE-labeled pmel CD8+ T cells (10:1 ratio, 72 h, 37 °C, 10% CO2) analyzed via Beckman Coulter Gallios flow cytometry and supernatant IFN-gamma ELISA. In vivo cytotoxicity in female C57BL/6 mice (n = 6/group; 100 ug VLP or molar-equivalent gp100 peptide + 25 ug CpG 1826 s.c. prime day 0, boost day 21; day 28 i.v. injection of 1 x 10^8 1:1 unpulsed CFSE-LO and 10 mM gp100-pulsed CFSE-HI splenocytes; lysis assessed 40 h later by flow cytometry). Day 30 cardiac-puncture serum anti-VP60 IgG ELISA (1:10,000 serum dilution, n = 3/group, Multiskan FC at 450 nm).
Key_Quantitative_Results: 15% w/v PVP mats electrospun at 24 kV and 0.1 mL/h yielded 100 nm to 5 um fibers containing intact ~40 nm VLPs (60 kDa VP60) after up to 7 days room-temperature dry storage. In vitro, gp100.2L VLP nanofibers induced ~100% standardized pmel T-cell proliferation and 111 ng/mL IFN-gamma (comparable to 116 ng/mL for free gp100 peptide; p < 0.0001 vs negative controls). In vivo, dissolved gp100.2L VLP nanofibers induced ~65% specific target-cell lysis compared to ~60% for fresh gp100.2L VLP in PBS (no statistically significant difference; free gp100 peptide induced minimal lysis and PBS/unmodified RHDV VLP nanofiber induced none), alongside comparable serum anti-VP60 IgG antibody titers.
ES_vs_SD_Comparative_Findings: No experimental spray-drying arm; author synthesis contrasts electrospinning (nanosecond ambient-temperature, atmospheric-pressure drying) against spray drying (nebulization shear stress and heated dehydration requiring complex multi-excipient systems for VLPs) and freeze-drying (long, costly, energy-intensive process that can cause VLP aggregation and attenuated immunogenicity), showing electrospinning preserves full VLP humoral and cell-mediated immunity.
Limitations_and_Research_Gaps: Proof-of-concept limited to a single water-soluble polymer (PVP K-90) requiring aqueous reconstitution prior to s.c. injection; stability assessed only up to 7 days at room temperature with silica gel (no long-term or ICH accelerated thermal stability); broader inter-animal lysis variance observed for the nanofiber group; no systematic optimization of electrospinning parameters, protein yield, trehalose stabilization, or direct experimental comparison against spray-dried or freeze-dried VLPs.
Research_Project_Takeaway: Validates electrospinning at 24 kV and 0.1 mL/h in 15% w/v PVP K-90/PBS as a low-stress dry-formulation strategy for ~40 nm VLP cancer vaccines, fully preserving particle structure and in vivo CTL (~65% lysis) and IgG immunogenicity without cold-chain dependence during short-term dry storage.

Autori: Katarzyna Olechno, Nina Katarina Grilc, Špela Zupančič, Katarzyna Winnicka
Dosage_Form_and_Route: Orodispersible nanofibrous mat / film (ODF) for oral cavity administration (8 cm2 dosage unit, ~15 um thickness, 2.5 mg target rupatadine fumarate dose).
Technology_Role: Sequential hybrid manufacturing: spray drying produces taste-masking ethylcellulose microparticles (MP-A-RUP), which are subsequently dispersed into an aqueous HPMC/PEO solution and electrospun into fast-disintegrating (<30 s) orodispersible nanofibrous mats.
API_or_Cargo: Rupatadine fumarate (RUP, ~99% purity, Xi'An Kerui Biotechnology Co., Ltd.; bitter-tasting antihistamine model drug).
Polymers_and_Carriers: Microparticle carriers: ethylcellulose aqueous dispersions Aquacoat ECD (24.5-29.5% EC, FMC BioPolymer) and Surelease E-7-19040 (25% EC, Colorcon Inc.). Nanofiber carriers: hypromellose (HPMC, MW 1260, Pharmacoat 606, Shin-Etsu) and polyethylene oxide (PEO, MW 2,000,000 [2M] and 4,000,000 [4M], Sigma-Aldrich).
Solvents_and_Additives: Purified/distilled water (sole solvent for both spray drying and electrospinning). Dispersion excipients present in commercial EC latices: sodium lauryl sulfate (0.9-1.7%) and cetyl alcohol (1.7-3.3%) in Aquacoat ECD; oleic acid (1.9%) and fractionated coconut oil in Surelease E-7-19040.
Formulation_Composition: Spray-dried microparticles: RUP:EC mass ratio 0.5:1 at 6% EC concentration (MP-A-RUP from Aquacoat ECD; MP-S-RUP from Surelease). Electrospinning screening: HPMC alone (3.5, 6.5, 9.5, 12.5% w/v) failed; optimal base: 6.5% w/v HPMC + 0.5% w/v PEO 2M. Final electrospun formulations in distilled water (stirred 24 h): F1 placebo (HPMC:PEO = 13:1), F2 pure RUP dispersion (HPMC:PEO:RUP = 13:1:2), F3 MP-A-RUP dispersion (HPMC:PEO:MP-A-RUP = 13:1:6). MP-S-RUP disrupted electrospinning and was excluded.
Electrospinning_Setup_and_Params: Fluidnatek LE-100 (Bioinicia, Paterna, Spain), vertical setup; 25 °C, 16% RH; applied voltage 15 kV; needle-to-collector distance 25 cm; grounded rotating drum collector covered with aluminum foil at 100 rpm.
Spray_Drying_Setup_and_Params: Buchi Mini Spray Dryer B-290 (Switzerland) with 0.7 mm conventional nozzle; inlet temperature 85 °C, outlet temperature 70 °C, aspirator flow rate 98%, dispersion feed rate 3.5 mL/min; ambient 20-25 °C, 40-50% RH.
Pre_and_Post_Processing: Aqueous EC dispersions diluted with purified water and blended with RUP prior to spray drying; aqueous HPMC/PEO/RUP or MP-A-RUP mixtures stirred for 24 h at room temperature for homogeneity before electrospinning; finished mats cut into 8 cm2 dosage units (~15 um thickness).
Characterization_Details: SEM (Carl Zeiss Supra35 VP, 5000x, 1 kV, uncoated; ImageJ n = 70 fibers) showed smooth, bead-free fibers with mean diameters of 340.21 +/- 31.16 nm (F1 placebo), 356.81 +/- 41.06 nm (F2 pure RUP with visible drug crystals), and 406.20 +/- 37.96 nm (F3 MP-A-RUP). DSC (Mettler Toledo DSC 1 STARe, ~7 mg, 25-300 °C, 10 °C/min, 50 mL/min N2) showed pure RUP Tm at 200.35 °C, amorphous placebo MP, shifted RUP Tm at 195.78 °C in spray-dried MPs, retained crystalline RUP peak in F2, and no detectable RUP melting peak in F3. Texture analysis (TA.XT plus, 20 mm gauge, 1 mm/s, 5 kg load cell, n >= 3) measured TS, Young's modulus, elongation at break, and tear resistance, revealing fragile, soft, fluffy mats with low stiffness, low tensile strength, and low tear resistance.
Performance_and_Bio_Assays: HPLC / UV-Vis / Assay & Content Uniformity; Tableting / Compaction / Disintegration; In Vitro Dissolution / Drug Release
Performance_Assay_Details: RUP assay/content uniformity by HPLC (Agilent 1200, Waters Spherisorb 5 um ODS1 4.6 x 250 mm, methanol:pH 3.0 NaH2PO4 buffer 35:65 v/v, 1.0 mL/min, 245 nm, r = 0.999, n = 3). Disintegration time assessed in vitro (Petri dish, 3 mL pH 6.8 phosphate buffer at 37 °C, n = 3) and in vivo in 6 healthy volunteers (Bioethics APK.002.112.2021, n = 3). In vivo taste-masking assessed in 6 healthy volunteers (30 s oral hold, 0-3 bitterness scale, n = 3). In vitro dissolution performed using Erweka DT 600HH mini-paddle/mini-vessel apparatus with enhancer cells (40 mL pH 6.8 phosphate buffer, 75 rpm, 37 +/- 0.5 °C, ultra-thin cellulose membrane cover, n = 3).
Key_Quantitative_Results: HPMC alone (3.5-12.5% w/v) produced beaded/clumped fibers, whereas 6.5% w/v HPMC + 0.5% w/v PEO 2M enabled uniform electrospinning (diameters: 340.21 +/- 31.16 nm F1, 356.81 +/- 41.06 nm F2, 406.20 +/- 37.96 nm F3). RUP loading was uniform at 2.52 +/- 0.33 mg per 8 cm2 mat (~15 um thickness, target 2.5 mg) with zero drug loss during electrospinning. All mats disintegrated in under 30 s. F3 (MP-A-RUP) was rated non-bitter to slightly bitter by volunteers and exhibited substantially slower RUP dissolution at pH 6.8 compared with rapid release from F2 (pure RUP).
ES_vs_SD_Comparative_Findings: Demonstrates complementary sequential coupling alongside formulation-dependent incompatibility: spray-dried Aquacoat ECD microparticles (MP-A-RUP) successfully integrated into aqueous HPMC/PEO electrospinning without losing taste-masking barrier function or <30 s disintegration, whereas spray-dried Surelease microparticles (MP-S-RUP, containing oleic acid and coconut oil) destabilized the electrospinning jet across all tested voltages, flow rates, and distances.
Limitations_and_Research_Gaps: Preliminary study yielding mats with poor mechanical properties (low tensile strength, low tear resistance, low Young's modulus—fragile, soft, and difficult to handle due to high solids loading); HPMC required PEO 2M as a spinnability aid; Surelease MPs could not be electrospun; numeric Table 1/Table 2/Figure 3 values were omitted from the available PMC full-text file; no stability or packaging studies conducted.
Research_Project_Takeaway: Proves a fully aqueous hybrid workflow—spray-drying rupatadine fumarate with Aquacoat ECD (85/70 °C) followed by electrospinning into 6.5% HPMC / 0.5% PEO 2M mats (15 kV)—achieving <30 s disintegration and effective human taste masking, while exposing mechanical fragility and EC-dispersion incompatibility (Surelease) as key barriers.
