Consolidation/post-processing: evaporation-induced self-assembly (EISA) at ~60 C on superhydrophobic/hydrophilic substrates or molds (~30 min) or ambient air drying; spray drying; lyophilization (2D cellulose nanosheet roll-up); direct ink writing (3D printing); oxidative stabilization and carbonization (lignin SPs)
Characterization_Methods: SEM; Rheology / Viscosity; Mechanical / Tensile Testing
Characterization_Details: Account/review summarizing structural and mechanical characterization across cited works: SEM images depict crumpled vs toroidal/spheroidal spray-dried ANF-particle SPs, conformal fibril wrapping (230 nm–1.15 um particles) vs cellular void-filling networks (40 um particles), and porous 3D-printed struts. Viscoelastic measurements show CNF-silica suspensions maintain near-constant properties until gelation (~3 wt% CNF, 20 wt% particles), where cantilever deflection reveals immediate residual drying stress onset. Force-strain curves of CNF-bound 200 nm SiO2 SPs (5% CNF) show an extended elastic-plastic regime (I), crack-reinforcing plateau (II), and densification (III) without complete breakage. Dried SPs resist wet-dry cycles, pH 4 and pH 9 aqueous media, and 100 C thermal aging for 1 week (fully wet SPs are weaker).
Performance_and_Bio_Assays: In Vitro Dissolution / Drug Release; Probiotic / Cell / Biologic Viability (CFU / Activity); Protein Adsorption / Swelling / Water Resistance
Performance_Assay_Details: Review of cited assays (specific dissolution media and analytical protocols not detailed in this Account): sodium salicylate release from 3D-printed CNF-bound silica grids with variable skin coverage; biocide release from biogenic silica nanoparticles vs SPs and CNF nanocomposites; thymol photodegradation kinetics under UV (lambda_max = 356 nm) and visible light in ~2 mm SPs; metabolic CO2 and ethanol production by immobilized yeast from sucrose and glucose; water disintegration/wet-strength testing (with WSA) of LP-CNF films and crossflow water permeability (>80 kPa); soil column outflow mobility testing.
Key_Quantitative_Results: CNF ultimate tensile strength 3 GPa, elastic modulus 40 GPa (EA up to 100 GPa), aspect ratio up to 100, smallest rigid unit ~100–150 nm; single charged CNFs (0.5–1.5 mmol/g carboxylate) gel at ~3 g/L vs ~10 g/L for uncharged bundled CNFs; >2.5 wt% CNF yields spherical SPs within 30 min at ~60 C; 5 wt% CNF prevents droplet merging at suspension interfaces; spray-dried ANF-particle SPs transition to corrugated morphology above ~1 vol% fiber per 10 nm particle diameter increase; 30% cotton-pollen bioplastic achieves 52.22 MPa tensile strength and 2.24 GPa Young's modulus; 2–8 wt% CNF boosts Pickering foamability up to 350% (wet stability >1 yr vs 5 min collapse without CNF); ~2 mm SPs restrict light penetration to outer 150 um, providing ~85% visible and 65% UV protection (>=2-fold retention vs nanoparticles); soil outflow <5% for SPs vs >95% for nanoparticles; carbonized lignin SPs adsorb 78 mg CO2/g; black bioinks achieve ~4% light reflectance.
ES_vs_SD_Comparative_Findings: No electrospinning comparison; compares spray drying against EISA casting, 3D printing, foaming, and lyophilization. Spray drying particle dispersions with amyloid nanofibers (ANFs) induces buckling instabilities and structural arrest during rapid drying to yield corrugated supraparticles above a linear threshold (~1 vol% fiber per 10 nm particle diameter), whereas pure particle spray drying yields non-corrugated toroidal/spheroidal/spherical SPs and EISA at ~60 C yields spherical SPs over ~30 min.
Limitations_and_Research_Gaps: Substantial non-pharmaceutical / general materials-science content: major sections focus on CO2 capture, carbonized lignin, superblack bioinks, sandy soil amendments, Pickering foams, bioplastics, paper diagnostic channels, and colloidal robotics, with only brief pharmaceutical/cargo-delivery examples (sodium salicylate 3D-printed grids, thymol photoprotection, yeast immobilization, cited ANF spray-dried SPs). No electrospinning is covered. Specific spray-drying operating parameters, drug encapsulation efficiencies, residual chemical checks, cytotoxicity/biocompatibility data, and ICH stability or in vivo PK data are absent. Authors explicitly highlight gaps in theoretical/computational modeling (e.g., Schweizer diffusion and graph theory) and scale-up/consolidation rate for commercial manufacturing.
Research_Project_Takeaway: Although predominantly a materials-science Account with broad non-pharmaceutical scope, it establishes useful physical design rules (mesh size, surface/contact crowding factors Ns/Nc, and ~1 vol% fiber per 10 nm particle size buckling threshold in spray drying) for using 1–15 wt% cellulose or amyloid nanofibers as universal cohesive binders in supraparticle carriers.

Research_Track: Track 2: Spray-Dried Nanofibers & Nanocellulose Excipients / Carriers
Titlu: Nisin-loaded gelatin microparticles for the enhanced bioactivity of bacterial nanocellulose
Autori: Maša Hren, Janja Trček, Aleksandra Šakanović, Hristina Obradović, Mateja Erdani Kreft et al.
Dosage_Form_and_Route: Bioactive bacterial nanocellulose (BnC) wound, periodontal, and surgical implant membranes functionalized with spray-dried nisin-loaded gelatin microparticles (topical / oral mucosal / implantable)
Technology_Role: Nano spray drying of gelatin microparticles (stabilized by dehydrothermal crosslinking and post-coated with nisin Z) to functionalize biosynthesized bacterial nanocellulose nanofibril membranes with dual antimicrobial and cytocompatible/mineralizing bioactivity
API_or_Cargo: Nisin Z (ultrapure >=95.0%, activity 38,000 IU/mg, 34-amino-acid class I lantibiotic antimicrobial peptide from Lactococcus lactis)
Polymers_and_Carriers: Bacterial nanocellulose (BnC, biosynthesized by Komagataeibacter melomenusus AV436T in grape pomace hydrolysate GP or RAE medium); Type B bovine skin gelatin (MW 15–80 kDa)
Solvents_and_Additives: Milli-Q water (18.2 MOhm·cm); D-mannitol (>=98%, tested at 20 wt% as spray-drying anti-agglomerant, omitted in optimal formulation); 0.5 M NaOH (membrane purification); RAE medium (glucose, peptone, yeast extract, citric acid, Na2HPO4·2H2O, agar, glacial acetic acid, absolute ethanol) or white Chardonnay grape pomace (GP) hydrolysate; 10x SBF salts (NaCl, KCl, CaCl2·2H2O, MgCl2·6H2O, NaH2PO4, NaHCO3)
Formulation_Composition: Spray-drying feed: 0.1, 0.5, and 1 wt% gelatin in Milli-Q water (40 C); optimal = 1 wt% gelatin without mannitol (also tested 0.5 wt% gelatin + 20 wt% mannitol, 0.5 wt% gelatin + 0.05 wt% nisin, and 1 wt% gelatin + 0.1 wt% nisin). Nisin post-loading: DHT-crosslinked Gsd dispersed in 150 ug/mL nisin Z solution at dry mass ratio gelatin:nisin = 5:1 (pH ~6). Membrane coating: 100 uL solution/dispersion containing 210.7 ug dry gelatin and 42.1 ug dry nisin per 1 cm2 BnC membrane (5:1 mass ratio)
Electrospinning_Setup_and_Params: N/A (no electrospinning performed; nanofibrillar network is biosynthesized bacterial nanocellulose produced by Komagataeibacter melomenusus AV436T)
Spray_Drying_Setup_and_Params: Büchi Nano Spray Dryer B-90 HP (open mode) with piezo-driven spray head (122 kHz) and electrostatic particle collector; tested small (down to 200 nm) and large (up to 5 um) nebulizers (large nebulizer selected as optimal); inlet temperature 120 C, spray velocity 70%, pump capacity 40%, air gas flow 100 L/min, device pressure 35 mbar; outlet temperature not reported in source
Pre_and_Post_Processing: Pre-processing: BnC biosynthesis by K. melomenusus AV436T (1 day shaking 180 rpm + 3 days static at 30 C in GP hydrolysate or RAE), purification in 0.5 M NaOH (80 C, 1 h), neutralization washing in distilled water, autoclaving in dH2O, and room-temperature air drying; gelatin dissolved at 40 C. Post-processing: dehydrothermal (DHT) crosslinking of spray-dried gelatin MPs at 140 C for 48 h; post-loading Gsd-DHT in 150 ug/mL nisin solution; pipetting 100 uL/cm2 coating onto BnC membranes and storing 1 h at room temperature
Characterization_Methods: FESEM; SEM; FTIR/ATR-FTIR; TGA; XRPD/XRD; XPS / EDX
Characterization_Details: FE-SEM (Carl Zeiss SUPRA 35 VP, 1 kV) shows spherical Gsd microparticles (1.083 +/- 0.622 um large nebulizer; 0.532 +/- 0.263 um small nebulizer), ~20% swelling after DHT to 1.31 +/- 0.53 um with reduced aggregation, and ~77% size increase after nisin coating to 2.36 +/- 1.69 um; BnC membranes show an interwoven nanofibril network fully film-covered by GN solution vs patchy microparticle-covered fibril networks in BnC-GNsd. ATR-FTIR confirms cellulose I bands, gelatin amide A/B/I/II/III peaks with no new covalent bond shifts upon DHT or nisin addition, and an intense ~1020 cm-1 phosphate (PO4^3-) band after 10x SBF mineralization. TGA (30–700 C, 10 C/min, N2) shows absorbed water loss (30–180 C, reduced 1% after DHT) and single-step gelatin degradation (210–494 C, ~75% mass loss). XRD (CuKalpha, 5–70 deg) confirms Ialpha-rich cellulose I (2theta = 14.5, ~21, ~23 deg), new CaP reflections (26, 29, 32 deg), and lower cellulose crystallinity index after mineralization. SEM-EDS identifies Ca/P ratios of 0.5 (MCPM), ~1.0 (brushite/pyrophosphate), ~1.3 (OCP/ACP), and 2.2 (ACP) as hydroxyapatite precursors.
Performance_and_Bio_Assays: HPLC / UV-Vis / Assay & Content Uniformity; Encapsulation Efficiency / Process Yield; Antimicrobial / MIC / Biofilm Assay; Cytotoxicity / Hemolysis / Biocompatibility
Performance_Assay_Details: TNBSA primary-amine UV-Vis assay (0.1 g sample, 0.5 wt% TNBSA pH 8.5, 40 C 3 h, 6 M HCl 60 C 1.5 h, absorbance at 335 nm on Varian Cary 50) quantified DHT crosslinking degree. In vitro biomimetic mineralization: 1x1 cm2 membranes immersed in 50 mL 10x SBF (pH 6.5) at 22–24 C for 6 h. Antimicrobial EUCAST (2016) disc diffusion on Mueller-Hinton agar incubated at 30 C (below 35 C gelatin melting point) for 24 h against S. aureus ATCC 29213, E. faecalis ATCC 29212, E. coli ATCC 25922, and P. aeruginosa ATCC 27853. Cytotoxicity: 7-day Trypan blue viability and inverted light microscopy on normal porcine urothelial (NPU) and human bladder carcinoma T24 cells on 1.5x1.5 cm membranes; 72 h free nisin (50–200 ug/mL) and 9-day modified BnC CellTiter-Glo 2.0 ATP luminescence viability assay on human gingival fibroblasts (HGF PCS-201-018, n=4, ANOVA/Tukey).
Key_Quantitative_Results: Optimal spray drying (1 wt% gelatin, large nebulizer) yielded ~5 g of 1.083 +/- 0.622 um spheres (vs ~0.3 g and 0.532 +/- 0.263 um with small nebulizer; ~0.2 g with 0.5% gelatin + 0.05% nisin). DHT crosslinking (140 C, 48 h) increased diameter ~20% to 1.31 +/- 0.53 um and raised TNBSA crosslinking degree from 23.1% (as-spray-dried) to 53.2% (reducing adsorbed water by 1% in TGA). Nisin post-coating (5:1, 150 ug/mL) increased diameter ~77% to 2.36 +/- 1.69 um. S. aureus inhibition zones: 12.3 +/- 0.47 mm (BnC-GN solution) and 11 +/- 0.58 mm (BnC-GNsd microparticles); no inhibition against E. faecalis, E. coli, or P. aeruginosa. NPU and T24 urothelial cell viability >90% across all BnC conditions. HGF viability increased ~20% with gelatin MPs (Gsd, GNsd) vs control (p=0.03 for BnC-GNsd), whereas BnC-GN solution reduced HGF viability by ~20%, an adverse effect eliminated by microparticulate nisin loading.
ES_vs_SD_Comparative_Findings: N/A (no electrospinning performed; nanofibers are biosynthesized bacterial nanocellulose). Directly compares spray-dried, DHT-crosslinked gelatin microparticles carrying nisin (BnC-GNsd) vs unstructured gelatin/nisin solution film coating (BnC-GN) on BnC membranes: both yield comparable anti-S. aureus inhibition (11.0 vs 12.3 mm), but microparticle structuring prevents the ~20% reduction in human gingival fibroblast viability caused by the solution coating and instead increases HGF viability ~20% over control.
Limitations_and_Research_Gaps: Explicitly noted by authors: lacks ISO 10993 standardized biocompatibility evaluation, broader antibiofilm and multi-strain/nisin-variant antimicrobial testing, and in vivo safety/efficacy studies. Additional observed gaps: nisin encapsulation efficiency (EE%) and quantitative in vitro drug release kinetics in physiological buffers were not measured (release only inferred from agar diffusion); disc diffusion was performed at 30 C rather than 37 C because gelatin melts at 35 C; direct co-spray drying of 1 wt% gelatin + 0.1 wt% nisin failed due to component interaction; no mechanical/tensile testing of BnC membranes or storage stability testing of nisin activity was conducted.
Research_Project_Takeaway: Nano spray-dried, dehydrothermally crosslinked gelatin microparticles (1.31 um, 53.2% crosslinked) post-loaded with nisin Z confer anti-S. aureus activity (11 mm zone) and CaP mineralization support to bacterial nanocellulose membranes while eliminating the ~20% fibroblast cytotoxicity seen with unstructured gelatin/nisin solution coatings.

Titlu: Development of Simvastatin-Loaded Particles Using Spray Drying Method for Ex Tempore Preparation of Cartridges for 2D Printing Technology.
Autori: Barbara Sterle Zorec, Rok Dreu
Dosage_Form_and_Route: Spray-dried polymeric dry emulsion microparticles for ex tempore 2D inkjet printing cartridges (personalized oral solid dosage forms)
Technology_Role: O/W emulsion spray drying with 5-factor DoE particle-size minimization and nanocellulose (NCC)/lactose antiadhesive stabilization to yield submicron-redispersible amorphous simvastatin/PCL microparticles for ex tempore 2D printing inks
API_or_Cargo: Simvastatin (SIM)
Polymers_and_Carriers: Polycaprolactone (PCL, 14,000 Da); antiadhesive/carrier excipients: nanocellulose (NCC, CelluForce), lactose (Mesh 200), calcium silicate (Florite R, CaSi)
Solvents_and_Additives: O/W emulsion phases: chloroform and purified water; surfactant: polysorbate 20 (Tween 20); antioxidant: ascorbic acid (AA); 2D blank ink redispersion media: propylene glycol (PG) and purified water mixtures (10/90, 50/50, 90/10 % v/v)
Formulation_Composition: Optimal emulsion EMU 2: organic phase 0.8 g SIM + 1.6 g PCL in 40 g chloroform; aqueous phase 4 g Tween 20 in 120 g water (3:1 w/w H2O:CHCl3, 20% dry matter before antiadhesives; also tested 4:1, 5:2, 2:1 ratios). Antiadhesives added prior to spray drying: 8% w/v lactose, 8% w/v NCC/lactose (25:75% w/w), or 2.5% w/v CaSi. Antioxidant: 0.2% w/w AA relative to total dry component weight. Theoretical SIM loading: 41.7–76.9 mg/g. Redispersion: 100 mg dry particles in 20 mL PG/water (10/90, 50/50, 90/10 v/v)
Electrospinning_Setup_and_Params: N/A (spray-drying only study; no electrospinning performed)
Spray_Drying_Setup_and_Params: Büchi Mini Spray Dryer B-290 with two-fluid nozzle (1.4 mm orifice, 2.20 mm cap). DoE ranges (46 runs): inlet T 110–170 C; drying gas flow 20–38 m3/h (50–100% aspiration); spraying rate 0.3–3.9 mL/min (1–13% pump); atomizing air 40–60 mm (473–742 L/h); nozzle-cap geometry 0–0.75 mm. Optimized E48 (combined product model): inlet T 170 C, drying gas flow 100%, nozzle pressure 60 mm, spraying rate 8.39%, nozzle geometry 0.2273 mm (also E47 collector model: 170 C, 84.85%, 40 mm, 13%, 0.3788 mm). Outlet temperature not reported in source; cyclone and collection vessel fractions collected separately
Pre_and_Post_Processing: Pre-processing: high-shear homogenization (IKA T25 Ultra-Turrax, 8000 rpm 5 min + 12,000 rpm 3 min) and high-pressure homogenization (APV 2000, 3 passes at 300 bar) to generate submicron O/W emulsion, followed by dissolution/suspension of antiadhesive (lactose, NCC/lactose, or CaSi). Post-processing: separate recovery of cyclone vs collection vessel powders; ex tempore redispersion in PG/water ink media via manual mixing or 2 min vortexing
Characterization_Methods: Particle Size (Laser Diffraction / DLS); SEM; DSC; Rheology / Viscosity; Electrical Conductivity / Surface Tension; Karl Fischer / Moisture Content
Characterization_Details: Zetasizer DLS gave EMU 2 droplet size 253.9 +/- 9.4 nm (PDI 0.179 +/- 0.017). Laser diffraction of dry powders (Mastersizer S, 5 bar feed pressure breaking clusters) gave d50 = 5.36 +/- 0.71 um (lactose), 5.47 +/- 0.88 um (NCC/lactose), and 14.81 +/- 0.11 um (CaSi) in collection vessel (slightly larger in cyclone: 6.11, 7.22, 21.51 um). SEM showed clustered structures for lactose and NCC/lactose vs large independent CaSi particles. DSC (Figs. S1–S6) showed crystalline SIM in pure powder/physical mixtures converted into an amorphous solid state in all spray-dried particles immediately and after 1 month at 25 C/40% RH and 40 C/75% RH. Loss-on-drying moisture content (Büchi B-302, 85 C, 15 min) ranged from 0.67% (NCC/lactose without AA) to 1.78% (CaSi with AA). Blank PG/water inks (10/90 to 90/10 v/v) showed dynamic viscosity 1–26 mPa·s and surface tension ~35–57 mN/m. Upon redispersion, NCC/lactose separated into submicron dispersions (d50 = 330–690 nm; 350 nm in 90/10 PG/water with vortex), staying <1 um over 1 month (except 50/50 water/PG agglomeration), whereas lactose redispersed at >5.6–10+ um and CaSi agglomerated to 1.3–2.8x dry size.
Performance_and_Bio_Assays: HPLC / UV-Vis / Assay & Content Uniformity; Encapsulation Efficiency / Process Yield; Physical / Chemical Stability (ICH / Accelerated)
Performance_Assay_Details: Waters Acquity UPLC-PDA (BEH C18 1.7 um 2.1x100 mm, 0.1% H3PO4/ACN/water gradient, 0.3 mL/min, 45 C, 238 nm; R2 = 0.9996) quantified SIM (4 min) and simvastatin hydroxyacid (6 min) for drug loading, EE%, and degradation (lactose and NCC/lactose washed in water and centrifuged at 3000 rpm for 10 min before CHCl3/MeOH extraction; CaSi directly dissolved in CHCl3/MeOH). 1-month dry particle chemical stability (+/- 0.2% w/w AA) evaluated at 25 C/40% RH and 40 C/75% RH. 1-month physical redispersion stability of 100 mg particles in 20 mL PG/water (10/90, 50/50, 90/10 v/v) evaluated by laser diffraction.
Key_Quantitative_Results: DoE optimized protocol E48 achieved combined d50 = 6.70 um (5.89 um collector, 6.60 um cyclone; CP model R2 = 0.7098, RMSE = 17.15 um). Without AA, SIM EE% peaked at 88.3% for NCC/lactose from collection vessel (DL 36.8 mg/g) vs CaSi (80.3% vessel / 72.9% cyclone, DL 61.7 / 56.1 mg/g) and lowest for lactose in cyclone (36.6%, DL 15.3 mg/g). Moisture content: 0.67% (NCC/lactose without AA), 0.70% (NCC/lactose with AA), 0.81% (CaSi without AA), 1.78% (CaSi with AA). After 1 month with AA at 25 C, SIM retention exceeded 85% in NCC/lactose (both locations) and >80% in lactose (88.22% cyclone, 82.94% vessel); at 40 C/75% RH, retention dropped to ~50% in NCC/lactose and 28.54% (cyclone) / 61.31% (vessel) in lactose. AA paradoxically accelerated SIM degradation in CaSi (hydroxyacid reached 4.3 ug/mL at 25 C and 7.48 ug/mL at 40 C vs 0.92 and 4.68 ug/mL without AA; <0.5 ug/mL in most other formulations). Redispersed NCC/lactose d50 = 330–690 nm (350 nm in 90/10 PG/water with vortex), remaining <1 um after 1 month in 90/10 and 10/90 PG/water.
ES_vs_SD_Comparative_Findings: N/A (spray-drying only study; no electrospinning performed). Internally compares spray-dryer sampling locations (collection vessel generally smaller size and higher EE% than cyclone walls) and three antiadhesives (NCC/lactose vs lactose vs CaSi), demonstrating that NCC/lactose uniquely provides the highest initial EE% (88.3%), lowest moisture (0.67–0.70%), strong AA stabilization (>85% at 25 C), and nanoscale redispersion (330–690 nm) for 2D inkjet printing.
Limitations_and_Research_Gaps: No actual 2D inkjet printing tests, printhead nozzle-clogging evaluations, or printed dosage-form content uniformity assays were performed (authors explicitly note NCC/lactose inks must be tested on a suitable inkjet printer). Residual chloroform (toxic ICH Class 2 organic solvent used in the O/W emulsion) was not quantified by GC. No in vitro dissolution or drug-release testing was conducted. Chemical stability was limited to 1 month (with ~50% degradation at 40 C/75% RH even with AA, and unexplained AA-induced SIM hydrolysis in CaSi). Minor text inconsistency: Fig 4 caption lists 45% RH vs 40% RH in text; DoE models had high NRMSE (56.93% and 58.12%).
Research_Project_Takeaway: Spray drying a PCL/simvastatin O/W emulsion with nanocellulose/lactose (25:75 w/w) and 0.2% ascorbic acid produces amorphous microparticles with 88.3% encapsulation efficiency, >85% 1-month room-temperature chemical stability, and submicron redispersion (330–690 nm) suitable for ex tempore 2D inkjet printing inks, though printability, dissolution, and residual chloroform analyses remain unverified.

Titlu: Effect of filler type on mechanical and biological properties of electrospun PLA used for bone tissue applications
Autori: Muna M. Kareem, K.E. Tanner
Dosage_Form_and_Route: Electrospun Polymer–Ceramic Composite Scaffold (Bone Tissue Engineering / Implantable)
Technology_Role: Electrospinning of PLA solutions incorporating commercial spray-dried hydroxyapatite (HA) filler vs sintered HA and β-TCP comparators to engineer bioactive bone scaffolds.
API_or_Cargo: Spray-dried hydroxyapatite (HA P218R, d50 = 4.02 µm), sintered hydroxyapatite (HA P220S, d50 = 3.59 µm), and β-tricalcium phosphate (β-TCP, d50 = 3.44 µm) ceramic fillers
Polymers_and_Carriers: Poly(lactic acid) (PLA, 3001D, NatureWorks, USA)
Solvents_and_Additives: Chloroform
Formulation_Composition: PLA dissolved in chloroform at 15 and 20 wt/vol% with ceramic fillers (HA P218R, HA P220S, or β-TCP) added to achieve 10 or 20 vol% in final spun fibrils.
Electrospinning_Setup_and_Params: Voltage: 13.7 kV; collector distance: 200 mm onto microscope slides, followed by drying (flow rate and needle gauge not reported in abstract).
Spray_Drying_Setup_and_Params: Commercial spray-dried hydroxyapatite filler (HA P218R, d50 = 4.02 µm, Plasma Biotal Ltd, UK) used as supplied; spray-drying parameters not reported in abstract.
Pre_and_Post_Processing: Pre-processing: dissolution of PLA in chloroform and dispersion of ceramic fillers. Post-processing: electrospun mats dried on microscope slides.
Characterization_Details: Fiber diameter measured by Nomarski optical microscopy with ImageJ software; tensile testing performed on 10 mm × 40 mm gauge length strips at 1 mm/s to determine Young's modulus, ultimate tensile strength, and strain at failure.
Performance_and_Bio_Assays: Protein Adsorption / Swelling / Water Resistance
Performance_Assay_Details: In vitro bioactivity and degradation assessed by soaking scaffolds in simulated body fluid (SBF) or distilled water and measuring wet and dry weight changes.
Key_Quantitative_Results: Filler d50: 4.02 µm (spray-dried HA), 3.59 µm (sintered HA), 3.44 µm (β-TCP). Both HAs yielded thicker non-uniform fibers and higher Young's modulus at 20% PLA without substantially reducing strength, whereas 15% PLA + HA reduced stiffness/strength and β-TCP reduced fiber diameter and degraded mechanical properties across both 15% and 20% PLA (exact modulus/strength numbers reside in omitted Table 1).
ES_vs_SD_Comparative_Findings: Hybrid filler-in-fiber evaluation: commercial spray-dried HA (P218R) behaved similarly to sintered HA (P220S) in reinforcing 20% PLA electrospun scaffolds, whereas β-TCP caused particle clustering that broke fiber continuity.
Limitations_and_Research_Gaps: Conference abstract omits Table 1 numerical mechanical/diameter values and SBF degradation weight-loss results; spray-drying was only the manufacturing origin of commercial HA P218R.
Research_Project_Takeaway: Shows that spray-dried hydroxyapatite microparticles can reinforce electrospun PLA bone scaffolds only when polymer concentration is sufficiently high (20 wt/vol%) to accommodate filler agglomeration.

Spray_Drying_Setup_and_Params: Büchi B-290 Mini Spray Dryer (Büchi Labortechnik AG, Flawil, Switzerland) with 0.5 mm nozzle and high-performance cyclone; inlet temperature: 170 °C; outlet temperature: 90 ± 5 °C; feed flow rate: 5 mL/min; atomizing gas flow: 473 L/h; drying air relative humidity (RH): 30-40%; aspirator rate: Not reported in source.
Pre_and_Post_Processing: Pre-treatment: BNC obtained by Komagataeibacter medellinensis fermentation and purification (2.41% aqueous dispersion); feed suspensions mixed by mechanical agitator at 1800 rpm for 20 min and homogenized with Ultra-Turrax T-25 at 10,000 rpm for 10 min prior to spray drying. Post-processing: None reported in source (collected via high-performance cyclone).
Characterization_Methods: SEM; TGA; FTIR/ATR-FTIR; Powder Flow / Bulk-Tapped Density; Karl Fischer / Moisture Content
Characterization_Details: ATR-FTIR confirmed preservation of cyanocobalamin structure and hydrogen-bonding interactions with BNC/MDX C-6 hydroxyls via a shift in the Co(III)-coordinated ν(C≡N) band at 2138 cm-1 (40-60% of BNC hydroxyl groups suggested to link with B12). SEM revealed spherical microparticles (2-8 μm, mostly 4-5 μm; ImageJ d10 ~2 μm, d50 4.5 μm for BNC_B12 and 5.2 μm for MDX_B12, d90 8-9 μm): BNC and BNC_B12 showed no aggregation and reduced roughness with B12, whereas MDX showed large agglomerates and solid bridges ('necks') that diminished upon B12 addition (surface shifted from flat to rough). Powder flow analysis (TA.XTplus) at ~8% moisture (105 °C oven drying) showed lower peak compression force and energy for BNC/BNC_B12 (~2.4 N) than MDX (2.8 N) and MDX_B12 (4.8 N), linked to bound water in crystalline BNC fibrils vs plasticizing free water in lower-MW branched amorphous MDX; however, Cohesion Index (CI) ranked flowability as MDX (7.7, free-flowing) > BNC (13.32, easy-flowing) > MDX_B12 (13.7, easy-flowing) > BNC_B12 (14.27, cohesive). TGA showed BNC elevated vitamin B12 degradation onset from 200 °C to 260 °C and Tmax from 274 °C (270 °C on p. 7) to 317 °C (+43 °C), whereas MDX_B12 onset matched pure MDX at 174 °C (Tmax 288 °C vs 293 °C for MDX).
Performance_and_Bio_Assays: Encapsulation Efficiency / Process Yield
Performance_Assay_Details: Spray-drying collection yield calculated gravimetrically as collected powder mass divided by feed solids mass. Powder flow and cohesion evaluated in triplicate using a TA.XTplus Texture Analyzer with Powder Flow Analyser rotating blade (50 mm/s, 140 mL bed, 3 conditioning + 3 test cycles); ANOVA and Duncan's multiple range test performed in SPSS v10.0. Encapsulation efficiency, loading capacity, dissolution/release, reconstitution, and storage stability assays were not performed.
Key_Quantitative_Results: Spray-drying yield: ~45% (BNC powders) and ~55% (MDX powders); moisture content: ~8% for all powders; particle size (SEM/ImageJ): 2-10 μm (mostly 4-5 μm), d10 ~2 μm, d50 = 4.5 μm (BNC_B12) and 5.2 μm (MDX_B12), d90 = 8-9 μm; peak compression force: ~2.4 N (BNC and BNC_B12), 2.8 N (MDX), 4.8 N (MDX_B12); Cohesion Index (CI): 13.32 (BNC), 14.27 (BNC_B12), 7.7 (MDX), 13.7 (MDX_B12); TGA degradation onset: 200 °C (B12), 260 °C (BNC and BNC_B12), 174 °C (MDX and MDX_B12); TGA Tmax: 274 °C (B12), 345 °C (BNC), 317 °C (BNC_B12, +43 °C vs B12), 293 °C (MDX), 288 °C (MDX_B12).
ES_vs_SD_Comparative_Findings: No electrospinning performed; head-to-head spray-drying comparison between bacterial nanocellulose (BNC) and maltodextrin (MDX) demonstrated BNC produced non-agglomerated microparticles with lower compression force/energy and up to 43 °C higher Tmax thermal protection for vitamin B12, whereas MDX gave higher collection yield (~55% vs ~45%) and lower baseline Cohesion Index (7.7 vs 13.32) prior to B12 loading.
Limitations_and_Research_Gaps: Explicitly noted by authors: encapsulation efficiency, loading capacity, reconstitution properties, powder density, and color were not quantitatively determined; no in vitro release, bioaccessibility, or bioavailability studies were conducted; no real-time/accelerated storage stability (light/oxygen) or short-time high-temperature industrial simulations (200-220 °C for 30-120 s) were performed; TGA thermal stabilization of ~1 wt% B12 may partially reflect matrix overlap (requires multi-rate model-free kinetics or DSC); low aqueous solubility, fermentation cost, and downstream scalability of BNC remain barriers; BNC_B12 was classified as cohesive (CI = 14.27).
Research_Project_Takeaway: Spray drying bacterial nanocellulose (BNC) with vitamin B12 yields non-agglomerated 4.5 μm spherical microparticles that increase B12 Tmax by 43 °C and avoid free-water plasticization observed in maltodextrin. However, pharmaceutical translation requires quantifying actual encapsulation efficiency and drug release, as well as addressing BNC_B12 cohesiveness (CI = 14.27) and lower process yield (~45%).

Research_Track: Track 2: Spray-Dried Nanofibers & Nanocellulose Excipients / Carriers
Titlu: Tuning the Physical Properties of Carboxylated Cellulose Nanocrystal (cCNC) Microspheres by Hybridizing with Silk Fibroin (SF)
Autori: Junqi Wu, Amelia Loesch‐Zhang, Mark P. Andrews
Dosage_Form_and_Route: Hybrid biopolymer microspheres for controlled drug delivery / small-molecule release and W/O emulsion stabilization (cosmetics, personal care, and pharmaceutical formulations)
Technology_Role: Spray drying of aqueous carboxylated cellulose nanocrystal (cCNC) and silk fibroin (SF) suspensions into surface-enriched hydrophobic core-shell-like microspheres with tunable β-sheet crystallinity (via methanol post-treatment) for controlled small-molecule release
API_or_Cargo: Methylene blue (MB, high purity, Alfa Aesar; model water-soluble cationic small-molecule drug/dye probe)
Polymers_and_Carriers: Carboxylated cellulose nanocrystals (cCNC, sodium salt form, 5.3 wt% aqueous suspension, Anomera Inc.) and Bombyx mori silk fibroin (SF, degummed and dissolved from Chinese silk cocoons, Treenway Silk)
Solvents_and_Additives: Ultrapure water (spray-drying medium); Na2CO3 (0.02 M) and LiBr (9.3 M) for SF extraction; methanol (HPLC grade, 20-100% / 80 wt% aqueous for post-treatment); acetone (99.6%, washing/AFM dispersion); for W/O emulsion test: ethanol (95%), NaCl, butylene glycol, C12-15 alkyl benzoate, silicone acrylate (KP 578), and Lauryl PEG-9 polydimethylsiloxyethyl dimethicone (KF-6038)
Formulation_Composition: Aqueous feed suspensions fixed at 0.5 wt% total solids across 100% cCNC, 2%, 5%, 10%, 20%, and 50 wt% SF in cCNC, and 100% SF (prepared by mixing 2 wt% SF solution with cCNC sodium salt suspension). For MB release: neat cCNC, untreated 2% SF-cCNC, and methanol-treated 2% SF-cCNC loaded at ~3.2 mg MB/g microsphere (100 mg beads in 45 mL of 78 mg/L MB overnight). For MB uptake: 5 mg microspheres in 3 mL of 10 mg/L MB. For W/O emulsion test: 0.2 g microspheres in 3 g oil phase + 7 g aqueous phase.
Electrospinning_Setup_and_Params: N/A (spray-drying only study)
Spray_Drying_Setup_and_Params: Büchi Mini Spray Dryer B-191 (BUCHI Corporation, New Castle, USA); inlet temperature: 175 °C; outlet temperature: 104 °C; pump speed: 30%; aspirator: 70%; nozzle diameter and atomizing gas flow: Not reported in source.
Pre_and_Post_Processing: Pre-treatment: B. mori silk cocoons (5 g) degummed in boiling 0.02 M Na2CO3 (2 L, 30 min), water-rinsed (3 x 20 min), dried overnight, dissolved in 9.3 M LiBr (20 wt% SF) at 60 °C for 4 h, dialyzed against water for 48 h (6 water changes), centrifuged twice at 4 °C (9000 rpm, 20 min), and vigorously stirred with cCNC suspension. Post-processing: methanol treatment (100 mg SF-cCNC microspheres left overnight in 100 mL of 80 wt% aqueous methanol — also tested at 20% and neat methanol and short exposure times down to 1 s — filtered and vacuum dried); for contact angle, ~0.5 g powder hydraulically pressed into 1 cm pellets at 27.58 MPa for 5 min.
Characterization_Methods: SEM; AFM; FTIR/ATR-FTIR; XPS / EDX; Contact Angle / Wettability
Characterization_Details: SEM (and DualBeam FIB-SEM cross-sectioning) showed morphology and size depended on SF content: neat cCNC gave wrinkled spheres (1.89 μm, 38.0% polydispersity) with a dense shell and porous interior; 2% SF gave elongated/horseshoe beads (2.5 ± 0.8 μm); 10% SF showed donut/collapsed hemispheres; 50% SF showed bimodal smooth inflated and collapsed/irregular beads; 100% SF yielded collapsed/broken shells (7.5 ± 1.8 μm) due to higher viscosity and outlet T (104 °C) >100 °C; FIB-SEM showed increased internal porosity from 2% to 20% SF. Ar+ XPS depth profiling (~5 μm over 10 cycles) confirmed SF surface enrichment: surface N was ~8% for 2% SF-cCNC (~53% SF surface coverage vs 15.1% for neat SF) and ~14% for 20% SF-cCNC (~93% coverage). Sessile drop water contact angle on pressed pellets rose from 27.5° (neat cCNC, rapid water absorption creep) to 60.4° (2% SF-cCNC). ATR-FTIR with amide I Fourier self-deconvolution showed spray-dried SF-cCNC adopted Silk I (1651 cm-1), while methanol triggered rapid (<1 s in 80% methanol) Silk II β-sheet formation (1627 cm-1; 20% aqueous methanol gave higher β-sheet yield than 80% methanol). AFM colloidal probe nanoindentation showed neat cCNC had the lowest Young's modulus; 10% SF-cCNC had bimodal stiffness (~30 and ~70 MPa), 20% SF-cCNC had ~15 & 50 MPa (protein plasticization), and methanol treatment shifted Young's modulus higher.
Performance_and_Bio_Assays: In Vitro Dissolution / Drug Release; HPLC / UV-Vis / Assay & Content Uniformity
Performance_Assay_Details: Methylene blue (MB) uptake and release kinetics quantified on a Thermo Scientific Evolution 260 Bio UV-Vis spectrophotometer at 665 nm (750 nm reference): for uptake, 5 mg microspheres immersed in 3 mL of 10 mg/L MB for 16 h (read every 10 min); for release, 100 mg microspheres loaded overnight in 45 mL of 78 mg/L MB (~3.2 mg/g), acetone-washed, and 5 mg immersed in 3 mL water for 72 h. W/O emulsion compatibility tested by dispersing 0.2 g cCNC or 10% SF-cCNC beads in 3 g oil phase (C12-15 alkyl benzoate, KP 578, KF-6038) and emulsifying with 7 g aqueous phase (water, 95% ethanol, NaCl, butylene glycol) at 2500 rpm for 5 min, then observing cast films by optical microscopy.
Key_Quantitative_Results: Microsphere diameter: 1.89 μm (38.0% polydispersity, neat cCNC), 2.5 ± 0.8 μm (2% SF-cCNC), 7.5 ± 1.8 μm (100% SF); XPS surface nitrogen: ~8% (~53% SF surface coverage) for 2% SF-cCNC and ~14% (~93% coverage) for 20% SF-cCNC (vs 15.1% neat SF); pellet water contact angle: 27.5° (neat cCNC) vs 60.4° (2% SF-cCNC); FTIR amide I peak shifted from 1651 cm-1 (Silk I) to 1627 cm-1 (Silk II) within 1 s in 80% methanol; AFM Young's modulus bimodal maxima: ~30 & 70 MPa (10% SF-cCNC) and ~15 & 50 MPa (20% SF-cCNC), shifting higher post-methanol; MB uptake equilibrium: 400 s (neat cCNC) vs lag time of 200 min (untreated 2% SF-cCNC) and ~300 min (methanol-treated 2% SF-cCNC) reaching equilibrium up to 1000 min; MB release (~3.2 mg/g loaded): burst release at t = 0 for all, neat cCNC released least over 72 h, untreated 2% SF-cCNC increased release, and methanol treatment slowed release rate and total released; 10% SF-cCNC dispersed uniformly in W/O emulsions up to 2 years.
ES_vs_SD_Comparative_Findings: No electrospinning performed; demonstrates that spray-drying aqueous cCNC nanorods with SF generates surface-enriched hydrophobic core-shell-like microspheres in one step without covalent modification, and explains dense-shell vs hollow/collapsed/donut particle formation via Péclet number and outlet temperature (104 °C > water boiling point).
Limitations_and_Research_Gaps: ChemRxiv preprint lacking spray-drying process yield and residual moisture data; contact angle required hydraulic pelletization at 27.58 MPa ('pancaking' spheres and introducing inter-bead pores); bimodal Young's modulus distributions at 10% and 20% SF indicate particle-to-particle heterogeneity; untreated 2% SF-cCNC unexpectedly released more MB than neat cCNC (attributed to possible SF/cCNC redistribution in water); tested only model dye MB without real APIs, encapsulation efficiency %, cytotoxicity/biocompatibility, or physiological-pH/in vivo studies; methanol post-treatment raises residual solvent toxicity concerns.
Research_Project_Takeaway: Co-spray-drying carboxylated CNCs with 2-20 wt% silk fibroin produces SF-surface-enriched hydrophobic microspheres (contact angle 60.4° vs 27.5°) without chemical modification, stabilizing W/O emulsions for up to 2 years. Post-spray-drying methanol treatment induces rapid (<1 s) Silk I-to-Silk II β-sheet crystallization that raises particle stiffness and retards small-molecule transport, though real-API encapsulation efficiency and residual methanol removal require validation.

Research_Track: Track 1: Head-to-Head Comparisons (Electrospinning vs. Spray Drying)
Titlu: Spray drying of pharmaceuticals and biopharmaceuticals: experimental optimization of process and formulation
Autori: Ahmad Ziaee
Dosage_Form_and_Route: Oral Amorphous Solid Dispersion (ASD) powders/fibers (Ibuprofen, BCS Class II) and Spray-Dried Biopharmaceutical Dry Powder (Lysozyme; pulmonary/general biologic delivery context)
Technology_Role: Chapter 3 directly compares Electrospinning (ES), Spray Drying (SD), and Rotary Evaporation (RE) for preparing Ibuprofen ASDs; Chapters 2 and 4 apply Design of Experiments (DoE) to Spray Drying (2-fluid and ultrasonic nozzles) for ternary small-molecule ASDs and biopharmaceutical (lysozyme) stabilization.
API_or_Cargo: Ibuprofen (IBU, BCS Class II model API; Form I); Lysozyme (model biomolecule/protein). (Review Ch. 1 and co-authored Ch. 5 also discuss insulin, measles/hepatitis B/meningitis A/Newcastle disease/Vibrio cholerae vaccines, AERAs-402, nicotinamide, carbamazepine, and saccharine.)
Polymers_and_Carriers: HPMCAS (Hydroxypropyl Methyl Cellulose Acetyl Succinate), HPMCP-HP55 (Hydroxypropyl Methyl Cellulose Phthalate), Kollidon VA 64 (copovidone); also lignin (Ch. 5 co-authored compaction study). (Ch. 1 review tables also cite sucrose, trehalose, mannitol, leucine, histidine, dextran, PVP, BSA, Eudragit, inositol, sodium citrate, and glycine.)
Solvents_and_Additives: Dichloromethane (DCM) and Methanol (MeOH) for Ibuprofen ternary ASD spray drying (Chapter 2); aqueous feed solutions for lysozyme spray drying (Chapter 4).
Formulation_Composition: Chapter 2: 16 DoE ternary ASD formulations of Ibuprofen (IBU), HPMCP-HP55, and Kollidon VA 64 (varying API:excipient ratio and DCM/MeOH ratio). Chapter 3: Binary IBU:HPMCAS and IBU:HPMCP-HP55 ASDs at 1:9, 3:7, 5:5, 7:3, and 9:1 ratios (10 wt.% IBU samples evaluated for BET specific surface area and dissolution). Chapter 4: Aqueous lysozyme formulations at varied feed solid concentrations.
Electrospinning_Setup_and_Params: Used in Chapter 3 to prepare IBU:HPMCAS and IBU:HPMCP-HP55 (1:9 to 9:1) nanofibrous ASDs; produced beads-on-string morphology at 1:9 IBU:HPMCP-HP55 and needle-like IBU crystals at 3:7 IBU:HPMCP-HP55 (exact voltage, flow rate, and distance values are in the full text outside the digest).
Spray_Drying_Setup_and_Params: Lab-scale BUCHI B-290 Mini Spray Dryer used for all experimental runs. Chapter 2 (16-run DoE): varied solid content, feed flow rate, inlet temperature, DCM/MeOH ratio, and API/excipient ratio. Chapter 4 (full factorial DoE on lysozyme): compared 2-fluid nozzle vs. ultrasonic nozzle, varying feeding rate, feed solid concentration, and outlet temperature (Tout; forced deactivation tested at Twb 35-45 °C and Tout 70-90 °C).
Pre_and_Post_Processing: Chapter 3 compared SD and ES against Rotary Evaporation (RE), with samples stored 9 months at room temperature in closed vials for stability assessment. Chapter 4 included solution and solid-state forced thermal deactivation studies (Twb 35-45 °C; Tout 70-90 °C). Chapter 5 summarized co-spray drying of lignin with surfactant for compaction and hot-melt extrusion (HME) of ibuprofen cocrystals.
Characterization_Methods: SEM; XRPD/XRD; DSC; FTIR/ATR-FTIR; Raman; BET / Porosimetry; Particle Size (Laser Diffraction / DLS); NMR / Solid-State NMR
Characterization_Details: Ch. 2: FTIR and 13C CP/MAS ssNMR (C1 shift from 183.0 ppm bulk to 177.2-177.9 ppm broad amorphous peak; C7 from 142.0 to 139.8-140.0 ppm) confirmed hydrogen bonding of IBU carboxyl groups; PXRD, DSC (20 °C/min), and D50 particle size. Ch. 3: PCA of Raman spectra (Form I IBU at 30/70 °C, melted at 80 °C, supercooled glass at 50 °C) assessed ASD homogeneity; DSC measured melting point depression and Tg; N2 adsorption/desorption isotherms (BET) measured specific surface area (10 wt.% IBU); SEM, FTIR, and PXRD (after 9 months RT storage). Ch. 4: SEM and D50 particle size (2-fluid vs. ultrasonic nozzle, R2=0.94), PXRD (amorphous for both nozzles), residual moisture content, and nozzle thermal mapping over 0-30 min.
Performance_and_Bio_Assays: In Vitro Dissolution / Drug Release; Physical / Chemical Stability (ICH / Accelerated); Probiotic / Cell / Biologic Viability (CFU / Activity)
Performance_Assay_Details: Ch. 2: Solubility and dissolution rate of spray-dried ternary IBU/HPMCP-HP55/Kollidon VA 64 ASDs vs. pure IBU. Ch. 3: Dissolution rate profiles of ES, SD, and RE IBU:HPMCP-HP55 and IBU:HPMCAS (1:9 ratio) ASDs; 9-month room-temperature stability in closed vials monitored by PXRD. Ch. 4: Retained enzymatic activity (%) of spray-dried lysozyme across DoE runs (2-fluid vs. ultrasonic nozzle, R2=0.84) and forced thermal deactivation kinetics (solution at Twb 35-45 °C; solid state at Tout 70-90 °C) fitted to an Arrhenius equation with inactivation rate constants and D-values.
Key_Quantitative_Results: Ch. 2: 16 DoE ternary IBU/HPMCP-HP55/Kollidon VA 64 formulations; 13C ssNMR C1 peak shifted from 183.0 ppm (bulk) to 177.2-177.9 ppm (amorphous ASD). Ch. 3: Tested 1:9, 3:7, 5:5, 7:3, 9:1 IBU:polymer ratios; ES achieved the highest API release rate and specific surface area at 10 wt.% IBU, while exhibiting needle-like IBU crystals at 3:7 IBU:HPMCP-HP55 and highest Raman PCA spectral spread; 9-month closed-vial RT PXRD stability assessed. Ch. 4: 2-fluid nozzle produced smaller particles (D50 intercept 5.44 ± 0.34 µm, R2=0.94) and higher retained lysozyme activity (intercept 87.5 ± 1.77%, R2=0.84) than ultrasonic nozzle (D50 intercept 13.44 ± 0.08 µm; retained activity intercept 46.87 ± 1.03%, ~50% lower activity). No substantial lysozyme inactivation in solution at Twb 35-45 °C, whereas solid-state heating at Tout 70-90 °C caused significant Arrhenius-type inactivation.
ES_vs_SD_Comparative_Findings: Direct head-to-head comparison of Electrospinning (ES), Spray Drying (SD), and Rotary Evaporation (RE) for Ibuprofen with HPMCAS and HPMCP-HP55 (1:9 to 9:1) showed: (1) ASD formation is solely formulation-dependent (API:excipient ratio and polymer choice, with HPMCAS outperforming HPMCP-HP55 due to higher melting point depression, higher Tg, and more H-bonding functional groups); (2) ASD homogeneity is technique-dependent—Raman PCA showed ES produced the least homogeneous ASDs (largest spectral spread/API clustering, risking crystallization nucleation on storage) compared to SD and RE; (3) ES yielded the fastest IBU release rate due to its nanofibrous morphology and higher specific surface area.
Limitations_and_Research_Gaps: 1) ES ASDs showed significant spatial inhomogeneity (API clusters by Raman PCA) that may act as nucleation sites and jeopardize long-term stability, plus beads-on-string (1:9) or needle-like IBU crystals (3:7) in HPMCP-HP55; 2) All SD experiments used a lab-scale BUCHI B-290 without pilot- or industrial-scale validation; 3) Ultrasonic atomization reduced lysozyme activity by ~50% and produced larger particles (13.44 µm vs. 5.44 µm) than 2-fluid atomization, and Tout 70-90 °C caused solid-state inactivation; 4) Future work needed on 3-fluid nozzles, pulmonary DPI particle engineering (2-5 µm), and high-dose variable DPI dosing.
Research_Project_Takeaway: Landmark head-to-head study proving that while Electrospinning maximizes specific surface area and dissolution rate of BCS Class II ASDs (Ibuprofen/HPMCAS or HPMCP-HP55), Spray Drying delivers superior molecular homogeneity (Raman PCA) essential for physical stability—alongside a QbD/DoE framework showing 2-fluid nozzle SD retains ~87.5% lysozyme activity versus ~46.9% for ultrasonic atomization.

Research_Track: Track 2: Spray-Dried Nanofibers & Nanocellulose Excipients / Carriers
Titlu: Drying kinetics of cellulose nanofibers suspensions
Autori: Belal Al Zaitone
Dosage_Form_and_Route: Dried cellulose nanofiber (CNF) porous microparticles / agglomerates (pharmaceutical excipient platform noted for sustained drug release, poorly soluble drug delivery, and capsule reinforcement; no API loaded experimentally).
Technology_Role: Single-droplet ultrasonic acoustic levitation used to mimic spray drying of aqueous CNF suspensions, isolating constant-rate and falling-rate drying kinetics and correlating process parameters with dried microparticle porosity and morphology.
API_or_Cargo: None loaded experimentally (blank CNF excipient study; text cites sustained drug release and poorly soluble drug delivery applications).
Polymers_and_Carriers: Cellulose nanofibers (CNF) 3.0% nominal (3.5 +/- 0.13% measured solid fraction) aqueous gel (University of Maine Process Development Center; nominal fiber diameter 50 nm, length up to a few hundred micrometers).
Solvents_and_Additives: Deionized distilled water (no additives or surfactants).
Formulation_Composition: CNF aqueous gel diluted with deionized distilled water and magnetically stirred for 30 min to obtain 2, 4, and 6 mg CNF/mL water suspensions.
Electrospinning_Setup_and_Params: Not used (study uses pre-formed botanical cellulose nanofibers rather than electrospinning).
Spray_Drying_Setup_and_Params: Simulated single-droplet spray drying in a 58 kHz ultrasonic acoustic levitator (piezo transducer + concave reflector standing wave) equipped with a heated gas chamber (up to 120 °C capability; tested at 20, 40, 60, and 80 °C) and surrounding airflow of 0.85 L/min to suppress outer acoustic streaming vortices; 1.0-2.0 uL droplets (~1.5 mm initial diameter) inserted axially via microliter syringe and monitored with a macro-lens CMOS camera and LED backlight.
Pre_and_Post_Processing: Raw CNF gel solid content verified by oven drying 10 samples at 60 °C for 10 h (3.5 +/- 0.13%); suspensions diluted and homogenized by magnetic stirring for 30 min; dried CNF particles collected post-levitation and fractured for internal SEM inspection.
Characterization_Details: SEM of intact and fractured dried CNF particles revealed non-spherical fibrous agglomerates (~200-300 um diameter) with consolidated surface fibers and an internal porous, randomly aligned network of 50 nm nanofibers folded by water surface tension. Online CMOS shadow imaging tracked normalized surface area decay (D/D0)^2, aspect ratio, and vertical drift in the acoustic field to calculate constant-rate d^2-law evaporation, falling-rate mass transfer via pressure-node vertical displacement (Eq. 3), and geometric particle porosity (epsilon = 1 - ms / [rho_s * Vp]).
Performance_and_Bio_Assays: None performed / Not reported in source
Performance_Assay_Details: No pharmaceutical dissolution, assay, or biological performance testing was conducted; evaluation focused strictly on single-droplet evaporation kinetics, vertical acoustic position tracking, particle porosity estimation, and SEM morphology.
Key_Quantitative_Results: Raw CNF gel solid content was 3.5 +/- 0.13% (60 °C, 10 h). Single 1.0-2.0 uL droplets (~1.5 mm initial diameter) at 2, 4, and 6 mg/mL dried at 20-80 °C into ~200-300 um non-spherical porous agglomerates. Evaporation rate increased with temperature (20 to 80 °C), following the d^2-law during the constant-rate shrinkage stage at <0.05% wt. CNF before transitioning to a constant-volume falling-rate regime tracked via upward drift in the acoustic field. Drying temperature had a moderate effect on mean porosity; notably, the paper contains an internal text contradiction on concentration effects (Section 3.2 states higher porosity occurs at lower initial CNF concentration, whereas the Abstract and Conclusions state packed particles form at lower concentration and porosity increases with higher CNF concentration).
ES_vs_SD_Comparative_Findings: No electrospinning comparison; models single-droplet spray drying of aqueous CNF suspensions via contactless acoustic levitation, contrasting spray drying with lyophilization and supercritical drying as CNF dewatering techniques.
Limitations_and_Research_Gaps: Single-droplet acoustic levitation uses millimeter-scale droplets (1.0-2.0 uL, ~1.5 mm), lower gas temperatures (20-80 °C), and far longer timescales (hundreds to >1000 s) than actual spray dryers; restricted to low CNF loadings (2-6 mg/mL) to avoid slurry viscosity issues; no pilot spray-dryer validation, no API loading or release experiments, and an unresolved internal contradiction in the text regarding the direction of CNF concentration effects on porosity.
Research_Project_Takeaway: Establishes single-droplet drying kinetics (58 kHz acoustic levitator, 20-80 °C, 2-6 mg/mL CNF) for spray-dried nanocellulose carriers, quantifying the shift from d^2-law shrinkage (1.5 mm to 200-300 um) to constant-volume falling-rate drying and porous folded-fiber microparticle formation.

Technology_Role: Single-needle and coaxial (core-shell) electrospinning of PLA and PCL-PLA fibrous scaffolds incorporating spray-dried hydroxyapatite (HA1) vs. sintered hydroxyapatite (HA2) or beta-tricalcium phosphate (beta-TCP) micro-fillers, plus 3D tubular rotating-needle collector electrospinning and BMP-2 delivery.

Polymers_and_Carriers: Polylactic acid (PLA, matrix/shell); Polycaprolactone (PCL, core in coaxial scaffolds)
Solvents_and_Additives: Chloroform and Acetone (2:1 chloroform:acetone solvent system for PLA/HA2 shell and chloroform:acetone for PCL core; pure chloroform and pure acetone also tested for PCL); fluorescent dyes FITC (shell labelling) and Rhodamine B (core labelling) for confocal microscopy.

Electrospinning_Setup_and_Params: Single-needle setup (syringe pump, needle, voltage supply, collector): 13.7 kV applied voltage, 1 mL/h flow rate for PLA and PLA/CaP optimization. Coaxial electrospinning: coaxial needle with two computer-controlled syringe pumps (20% PCL core, 15% PLA/20% HA2 shell) at 1:3, 2:3, and 3:3 core:shell flow rate ratios. 3D tubular electrospinning: rotating needle collector driven by a motor with G16 and G21 needles defining internal diameter.
Spray_Drying_Setup_and_Params: Spray drying was not performed in-house in this thesis; pre-fabricated spray-dried micro-hydroxyapatite powder (HA1, higher surface area; cited from Zhang and Tanner, 2008) was incorporated as a bioactive ceramic filler inside electrospun PLA fibers and compared directly against sintered HA (HA2) and beta-TCP.
Pre_and_Post_Processing: Resin embedding and sectioning (longitudinal and transverse) for SEM and TEM core-shell inspection; immersion in distilled water, Simulated Body Fluid (SBF, 1-28 days for 2D; up to 12 weeks for 3D tubular), or PBS (12 weeks for 3D) for degradation and bioactivity; FITC/Rhodamine B fluorescent dye labelling for confocal microscopy.
Characterization_Methods: SEM; TEM; Micro-CT / Confocal Microscopy; BET / Porosimetry; TGA; FTIR/ATR-FTIR; XPS / EDX; Mechanical / Tensile Testing
Characterization_Details: Optical/Nomarski microscopy; SEM (fiber morphology, fractured fibers, resin-embedded longitudinal/transverse sections, and post-SBF HCA precipitation); TEM (core-shell thickness, continuous vs. discontinuous shell, HA nano-fragments); LSCM (Rhodamine B-labelled PCL core, FITC-labelled PLA/HA2 shell); mercury porosimetry (Ch. 6) and gravimetric porosity/apparent density (87.86-91.41% porosity, 0.117-0.190 g/cm3); TGA (Tonset, Td, residue wt% before/after 28d SBF); FTIR; EDX (Ch. 7); tensile mechanical testing (Young's modulus, UTS, strain at failure before and after 14d SBF or 12w PBS/SBF).
Performance_and_Bio_Assays: In Vitro Dissolution / Drug Release; Cytotoxicity / Hemolysis / Biocompatibility; Protein Adsorption / Swelling / Water Resistance
Performance_Assay_Details: In vitro degradation (dry weight loss and water uptake in distilled water, SBF over 1, 2, 4, 7, 14, 21, 28 days, and PBS/SBF over 12 weeks for 3D tubular scaffolds); SBF bioactivity assay (hydroxycarbonate apatite [HCA] deposition via SEM/EDX/FTIR); mechanical retention after 14 days SBF (single-needle mats too fragile at day 28) and 12 weeks PBS/SBF (3D coaxial); BMP-2 protein release over 96 hours; 21-day cell culture attachment and spreading assay.
Key_Quantitative_Results: Only 15 and 20 wt% PLA with 10 or 20 vol% CaP (22.08 and 38.93 wt% HA by TGA) produced electrospun scaffolds; porosity ranged from 87.86 ± 1.66% to 91.41 ± 2.87% (apparent density 0.117-0.190 g/cm3). Spray-dried HA1 improved thermal stability (TGA Tonset 280.6-297.7 °C, Td 409.1-427.2 °C) vs. sintered HA2 (Tonset 227.6-247.1 °C, Td 379.9-405.8 °C) and electrospun unfilled PLA (Tonset 236.0 °C, Td 400.6 °C). After 14d SBF immersion, Young's modulus of 15% PLA dropped to 40.16 ± 3.05 MPa (0% filler), 24.57 ± 2.54 MPa (10% HA1), 20.89 ± 1.60 MPa (20% HA1), 29.06 ± 1.52 MPa (10% HA2), and 32.86 ± 4.90 MPa (20% HA2), while 20% PLA retained 48.32 ± 5.17 MPa (0%) vs. 32.31-45.03 MPa (HA-filled); all single-needle HA scaffolds lost mechanical integrity by 28d SBF. Coaxial PCL-core/PLA-HA2 scaffolds increased tensile strength and strain at failure, showed gradual mechanical decay over 12 weeks in PBS/SBF, released 12.8-13.6% BMP-2 gradually over 96 h, supported cell attachment/spreading for 21 days, and formed large apatite layers after 12 weeks in SBF.
ES_vs_SD_Comparative_Findings: Evaluates pre-formed spray-dried micro-HA (HA1, higher specific surface area) against sintered HA (HA2) and beta-TCP as fillers within electrospun PLA and coaxial PCL-PLA fibers (rather than comparing ES and SD processes head-to-head). Higher surface area of spray-dried HA1 increased composite thermal stability (higher TGA Tonset and Td) relative to sintered HA2, did not significantly change SBF bioactivity rate, but caused a greater reduction in in vitro mechanical properties after 14 days SBF immersion compared to HA2.
Limitations_and_Research_Gaps: 1) Adding CaP fillers significantly reduced mechanical properties vs. unfilled PLA and increased fiber diameter and non-uniformity (with beta-TCP forming agglomerations); 2) Single-needle PLA/HA mats lost mechanical integrity within 28 days of SBF immersion and showed lower apatite formation than nano-HA due to lower surface area of micro-HA and limited surface exposure; 3) Coaxial spinning yielded occasional discontinuous shells, twin/grooved fibers, hollow fibers, or coreless PLA fibers, and rotating-needle 3D collection increased fiber non-uniformity in HA-containing scaffolds.
Research_Project_Takeaway: Demonstrates that incorporating spray-dried micro-hydroxyapatite (HA1) into electrospun PLA improves composite thermal stability over sintered HA2, while transitioning to coaxial PCL-core/PLA-HA-shell electrospinning preserves mechanical integrity over 12 weeks in PBS/SBF, supports 21-day cell spreading, enables extensive SBF apatite mineralization, and provides sustained 96-h BMP-2 release (12.8-13.6%).

Pre_and_Post_Processing: Continuous collection (1-1.7 m cellulose/synthetic/fiberglass/foil substrate webs, PP collecting fleece with doctor blade removal, electrostatic deposition onto moving pullulan film, or cyclone collection causing partial fiber fragmentation); milling/grinding (vibrating mill after fine cutting, knife grinder, hammer mill, cutting mill, oscillating sieve mill; grindability improved with mannitol or glucose); Turbula mixing with fillers for capsules; blending with fillers/excipients and rotary tableting; non-conventional folding/rolling/cutting/coating, elongated rod-die stripping, and direct mat compression into mono-/three-layered tablets and minitablets

Performance_and_Bio_Assays: In Vitro Dissolution / Drug Release; HPLC / UV-Vis / Assay & Content Uniformity; Tableting / Compaction / Disintegration; Physical / Chemical Stability (ICH / Accelerated); Antimicrobial / MIC / Biofilm Assay; In Vivo PK / Efficacy
Performance_Assay_Details: In vitro dissolution testing at gastric, neutral (pH 6.8), and colonic pH, plus biphasic/sustained release and reconstitution testing (voriconazole/SBE-beta-CD comparable to commercial freeze-dried product); HPLC impurity quantification after 1-month storage (MES carvedilol); rotary tableting testing (weight variation, hardness, friability, disintegration time, dissolution); antimicrobial pathogen testing (metronidazole nanofibers); and in vivo bioavailability testing (flubendazole vs crystalline API)
Key_Quantitative_Results: Scale-up productivity benchmarks: SNES 0.01-1 g/hr (aqueous 0.02-0.5 g/hr; DCES ~5 mL/hr) increased to 42.5-56.7 g/hr (electroblowing), 60 g/hr (corona ES and high-speed rotary spinning), 117 g/hr (C-ACES, up to 1,200 mL/hr), 240-270 g/hr (nozzle-based high-speed ES at 40,000 rpm with cyclone), and 450 g/hr (free-surface high-speed ES; 350 g/hr for tableted itraconazole/PVPVA64). MES carvedilol/Eudragit E processing temperature dropped by 20 C (155 C to 135 C) with plasticizers, lowering 1-month HPLC impurities while completing release in 2 min. Fast-dissolving PVP fibers released 85% in 20 s; PVA fibers released 100% in seconds; PVA/PEO/metronidazole released 84% in 2 h
ES_vs_SD_Comparative_Findings: ES is highlighted as a continuous, low-energy, ambient-temperature/atmospheric-pressure alternative to spray drying and freeze drying that preserves thermolabile biopharmaceuticals (proteins, enzymes, vaccines, probiotics). In a direct comparison cited (Soti et al., 2015), electroblowing of itraconazole/Eudragit E reached 50-56.7 g/hr and yielded an ASD with superior physical stability over spray-dried samples. Nozzle-based high-speed ES also adopted spray-drying-style cyclone collection for continuous powder recovery and fragmentation

Research_Project_Takeaway: Maps the complete industrial scale-up landscape for pharmaceutical electrospinning (up to 240-450 g/hr via high-speed/C-ACES + cyclone recovery and mill-blend-tablet lines) and provides direct rationale for ES advantages over spray drying in ASD stability and gentle biologic drying

Characterization_Methods: SEM; TEM; AFM; XRPD/XRD; DSC; TGA; FTIR/ATR-FTIR; Particle Size (Laser Diffraction / DLS); Rheology / Viscosity; Electrical Conductivity / Surface Tension
Characterization_Details: Section 5 specifies laser diffraction for particle size distribution (number/volume %), SEM for size and shape, TEM for structures <200 nm, AFM for surface topography and mechanical properties, XRD for crystalloid phase, FTIR-ATR for shell composition and external degradation, DSC for endothermic/exothermic transitions and melting/solidifying enthalpy, TGA for thermal stability/weight loss, plus solution viscosity, surface tension, electrical conductivity, solubility, and hygroscopicity
Performance_and_Bio_Assays: In Vitro Dissolution / Drug Release; Encapsulation Efficiency / Process Yield; Physical / Chemical Stability (ICH / Accelerated); In Vivo PK / Efficacy
Performance_Assay_Details: Encapsulation efficiency and product yield quantification; controlled release testing in deionized water (pH 5.6), simulated gastric fluid vs room temperature, and in vitro intestinal digestion conditions (evaluating dissolution fluid, osmotic pressure, enzymes, and pH); thermal stability (up to 188 C), shelf-life storage (4-6 months), and UV/UVA photoprotection assays; and in vivo carrageenan-induced paw edema anti-inflammatory assay in albino rats
Key_Quantitative_Results: Spray drying: vitB1 EE 66-100% and product yield 17-52%; folic acid yields 49.8% (pectin) and 44.4% (modified starch) with complete release <2 h at pH 5.6; vitC 90% EE (9.1 um GA microparticles, stable up to 188 C); vitB12 yields 27-50% (4-month shelf life) and ~57% (modified chitosan, 6-month stability), and 82% EE in wrinkled zein microcapsules (8.32% w/w loading); vitB1+vitB6 ferulic acid-grafted chitosan microspheres (4.5-4.8 um) gave 52.3-56.9% paw edema inhibition in rats. Electrospinning/electrospraying: folic acid in amaranth:pullulan achieved 95.6% EE with zero degradation after 2 h UV exposure; zein microbeads (~3 um) and ribbon fibers achieved >90% vitB12 EE
ES_vs_SD_Comparative_Findings: Spray drying is simple, fast, economically viable, and easily scaled up for industry, but relies on high temperatures that risk degrading thermolabile vitamins and can produce wrinkled capsules or moderate product yields. Electrospinning/electrospraying requires no high temperature or harsh chemicals, preserves thermolabile vitamins, produces smaller-diameter high-surface-area structures with superior encapsulation efficiency (e.g., WPC/folic acid achieved higher EE via ES than nanospray-drying; zein/vitB12 achieved >90% EE via ES vs 82% via SD), and generally yields faster release profiles than spray drying
Limitations_and_Research_Gaps: Tables 1-4 were stripped in the PMC text extraction. Scientifically, spray drying exposes heat-sensitive vitamins to thermal degradation; simple electrospinning/electrospraying suffers from low productivity due to low biopolymer solubility and poor viscoelasticity, requiring multiaxial/emulsion scale-up and strict temperature/humidity control; monolithic ES suffers from burst release unless hydrophobic shells or coaxial/W-O emulsion structures are used; and food/nutraceutical ES remains less explored than pharmaceutical applications
Research_Project_Takeaway: Provides direct ES vs SD encapsulation efficiency, morphology, and release-rate comparisons for labile water-soluble vitamins across polysaccharide and protein wall materials

API_or_Cargo: Apalutamide (Erleada), elexacaftor + tezacaftor + ivacaftor (Trikafta), doravirine + lamivudine + tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (Delstrigo), tezacaftor + ivacaftor (Symdeko), lumacaftor + ivacaftor (Orkambi), posaconazole (Noxafil), ivacaftor (Kalydeco), vemurafenib (Zelboraf), telaprevir (Incivek), plus mechanistic study APIs progesterone, carbamazepine, and itraconazole

Formulation_Composition: Marketed HPMCAS ASDs: Erleada (apalutamide 60 mg, 240 mg IR tablets); Trikafta (elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor tablets & granules); Delstrigo (bilayer tablet: doravirine 100 mg HPMCAS ASD layer + lamivudine 300 mg / tenofovir disoproxil fumarate 300 mg co-granulated layer); Symdeko (tezacaftor 100 mg / ivacaftor 150 mg + ivacaftor 150 mg); Orkambi (lumacaftor 200 mg / ivacaftor 125 mg); Noxafil (posaconazole HPMCAS delayed-release tablet via HME); Kalydeco (ivacaftor spray-dried HPMCAS ASD); Zelboraf (vemurafenib:HPMCAS-LF 30:70 w/w microprecipitated bulk powder); Incivek (telaprevir 375 mg spray-dried HPMCAS ASD in 1 g tablet)
Electrospinning_Setup_and_Params: Mentioned briefly in the Abstract as one of the ASD preparation techniques (alongside HME, spray drying, supercritical fluid technology, and KinetiSol) that disrupt the drug crystal lattice and arrest molecular motion; no ES apparatus or process parameters are detailed
Spray_Drying_Setup_and_Params: Feed pump matched to feed viscosity/atomizer, atomizing nozzle into large-diameter drying chamber (droplet residence time typically milliseconds), hot drying gas (air, turbulent or laminar) with strict inter-batch temperature and humidity control, particle separation via reverse-flow cyclones and bag filters, exhaust HEPA filtration, and secondary drying to remove residual solvent. Critical variables: solution viscosity, total solid content, inlet/outlet temperatures, nozzle selection, and drying gas flow rate. Used commercially for Erleada, Trikafta, Delstrigo, Symdeko, Kalydeco, and Incivek
Pre_and_Post_Processing: Pre-blending of spray-dried intermediate (SDI), granulation, roller compaction (Delstrigo), secondary drying (Incivek, Zelboraf), extra-granular blending, lubrication, tablet compression (including bilayer compression), and film coating; for HME (Noxafil): feeding, melting/plasticizing, conveying/mixing, venting, stripping, and downstream processing; for Zelboraf precipitation: filtration, repeated washing, vacuum drying, and milling
Characterization_Methods: Particle Size (Laser Diffraction / DLS); Rheology / Viscosity
Characterization_Details: Tables 1-4 were omitted in the PMC text extraction. Text identifies droplet/particle size distribution, feed solution viscosity, total solid content, final moisture content, residual solvent levels, Log P, pKa, melting temperature (Tm), and glass transition temperature (Tg) as critical physicochemical and process attributes
Performance_and_Bio_Assays: In Vitro Dissolution / Drug Release; Physical / Chemical Stability (ICH / Accelerated); Mucoadhesion / Permeation / Ex Vivo; In Vivo PK / Efficacy
Performance_Assay_Details: In vitro dissolution and supersaturation/recrystallization-inhibition assays; rat jejunal perfusion (progesterone/HPMCAS), Caco-2 monolayer, and dialysis membrane permeation studies (carbamazepine with HPMCAS vs Poloxamer 407; itraconazole with bile salts); preclinical bioavailability in rats and beagle dogs; and human Phase-I/III PK (Cmax, AUC, Tmax, fed/fasted food-effect) and clinical tumor-regression efficacy
Key_Quantitative_Results: Over 20 FDA-approved ASD products in the prior 12 years (8 using HPMCAS noted in Section 3, 9 subsections detailed): Kalydeco/Symdeko ivacaftor HPMCAS SD ASD raised solubility from 1 ug/mL (polymorph B) to 67.4 ug/mL and rat relative bioavailability from 3-6% (crystalline) to ~100%, giving fed human AUC 10,600 ng*h/mL and Cmax 768 ng/mL; Erleada steady-state Cmax 6 ug/mL and AUC 100 ug*h/mL; Orkambi capsule Cmax/AUC0-inf 1.4x higher than suspension (Tmax 3 h vs 4 h), ivacaftor exposure +2.5-3.4x with fatty food; Incivek (375 mg telaprevir in 1 g tablet, crystalline solubility 4.7 ug/mL) showed 3-4x higher AUC and Cmax in fed vs fasted state; Zelboraf (30:70 vemurafenib:HPMCAS-LF) achieved ~30x dissolution, ~5x plasma concentration, and substantial tumor regression (vs none up to 1,600 mg conventional dose)
ES_vs_SD_Comparative_Findings: No direct ES vs SD comparison is presented (ES is only listed among ASD techniques). Between the two primary industrial methods reviewed, SD accommodates thermolabile APIs via millisecond droplet solvent evaporation, whereas HME is continuous and solvent-free but requires higher energy input and excludes thermally labile drugs
Limitations_and_Research_Gaps: Tables 1-4 were stripped in the PMC text extraction. Key industrial/clinical gaps reported: SD chamber-wall adherence losses for expensive APIs, secondary drying requirements for residual organic solvents, and tight inter-batch drying-air T/RH control; HME exclusion of thermolabile drugs; limited clinical data on HPMCAS immunomodulatory, genotoxic, or gut-microbiome effects; and poor in vitro-in vivo correlation (IVIVC) / PBPK predictability for translating in vitro dissolution to human oral bioavailability across fed/fasted bile-salt states
Research_Project_Takeaway: Establishes commercial/regulatory benchmarks for spray-dried HPMCAS ASDs (FDA-approved products, cyclone/HEPA/secondary-drying architecture, roller compaction/tableting, and IVIVC/residual-solvent hurdles) as the clinical bar for electrospun HPMCAS systems

Titlu: A Review on Fast Dissolving Systems: From Tablets to Nanofibers
Autori: Sara Bahrainian, Mohammadreza Abbaspour, Maryam Kouchak, Pooria Taghavi Moghaddam
Jurnal_Sursa: Jundishapur Journal of Natural Pharmaceutical Products
Dosage_Form_and_Route: Oral fast-dissolving systems (FDS) for oral cavity/intraoral, buccal, and sublingual local or systemic delivery (bypassing first-pass metabolism): fast-dissolving tablets (FDTs/ODTs), fast-dissolving films/strips/wafers/patches (FDFs), and fast-dissolving electrospun nanofiber mats/films
Technology_Role: Comparative pharmaceutical review of oral fast-dissolving dosage forms (tablets, films, and nanofibers) covering preparation methods—including spray drying (for FDT powder production prior to compression) and electrospinning (for ultrafast-dissolving amorphous nanofiber mats)—excipients, and functional evaluation methods
API_or_Cargo: Acetaminophen, caffeine, indomethacin, ibuprofen, diclofenac, diclofenac sodium, donepezil (donepezil HCl), sumatriptan (sumatriptan succinate), metoclopramide, dimenhydrinate, tetracycline HCl, ascorbic acid, nicotinamide, verapamil, meclizine HCl, riboflavin, granisetron HCl, tizanidine HCl, triclosan, naproxen, ziprasidone HCl, paracetamol, salbutamol sulphate, valdecoxib, griseofulvin, lamotrigine, venlafaxine HCl, metformin HCl, aspirin, clotrimazole, imiquimod, quercetin, prochlorperazine, citalopram HBr, loratadine, miconazole, nitrofurazone, cetirizine HCl, feruloyl-oleyl-glycerol
Polymers_and_Carriers: PLGA, poly(lactide-caprolactone), chitosan (and chitosan lactate), collagen, cellulose acetate phthalate, PVA, PEG, PVP, HPMC, HPC, maltodextrin, Soluplus, Eudragit L 100-55, poly(ethylene-co-vinylacetate), PLA, microcrystalline cellulose (MCC), modified starch, crospovidone, croscarmellose
Solvents_and_Additives: Polar/aqueous/organic solvents; saliva-stimulating agents (ascorbic acid, nicotinamide); flavoring agents; coloring agents/opacifiers; surfactants; plasticizers (for films); superdisintegrants (5-10%: MCC, HPMC, modified starch, crospovidone, croscarmellose); binders (1-2%); hydrophilic lubricants (sodium/potassium benzoate preferred over hydrophobic calcium/magnesium stearate); fillers; beta-cyclodextrin; sorbitan monooleate
Formulation_Composition: Tablets require superdisintegrants (5-10%), binders (1-2%), lubricants, and fillers; films require polymers and plasticizers; fast-dissolving nanofibers can be fabricated using only API and polymer (plus optional surfactants, nanoparticles, or microemulsions), reducing excipient side effects and cost
Electrospinning_Setup_and_Params: Spinning solution loaded into a syringe with a stainless steel capillary metal-hub needle (positive high-voltage electrode) facing a grounded metal collector of varied size/shape. Increasing voltage forms a Taylor cone and ejects a fiber jet that thins to nanoscale and dries via solvent evaporation during flight (or melt electrospinning solidified by cooling). Key parameters: applied voltage, needle-to-collector distance, syringe feed rate (bubble-free), polymer type/concentration. Alternative nanofiber methods listed in Table 2: drawing, template synthesis, phase separation, self-assembly
Spray_Drying_Setup_and_Params: Listed under FDT tablet preparation (Section 3.4.1.2): an aqueous solution containing the drug, a specific matrix, and other excipients is sprayed to vaporize the solvent and produce a fine powder, which is subsequently compressed into fast-dissolving tablets
Pre_and_Post_Processing: Spray-dried powders undergo tableting compression into FDTs; other FDT methods include lyophilization, molding, sublimation, mass extrusion, and direct compression. Films use solvent casting, semi-solid casting, hot melt extrusion, rolling, solid dispersion extrusion, and compaction. Electrospun nanofibers are collected directly as films/strips in desired sizes/shapes or combined with microemulsions/nanoparticles
Characterization_Details: Table 3 lists evaluation parameters for tablets (thickness, hardness, crushing strength, friability, wetting time, uniformity of dispersion, taste/mouth sensation) and films/nanofibers (morphology study, fiber diameter for nanofibers only, thickness, organoleptic/taste evaluation, tensile strength, tear resistance, elastic modulus, percentage elongation, folding endurance, water absorption ratio, swelling property). Section 3.6 notes high-speed camera filming for ultra-fast disintegration/dissolution
Performance_and_Bio_Assays: In Vitro Dissolution / Drug Release; Tableting / Compaction / Disintegration; Mucoadhesion / Permeation / Ex Vivo; Protein Adsorption / Swelling / Water Resistance
Performance_Assay_Details: In vitro dissolution (low-volume 5-10 mL media for films and nanofibers, filmed by high-speed camera) and disintegration time testing across FDTs, films, and nanofibers; tablet hardness, crushing strength, friability, and wetting time; film/nanofiber water absorption ratio and swelling property; organoleptic/taste evaluation; and oral mucosal permeation/mucoadhesion performance
Key_Quantitative_Results: Table 4 benchmarks: Fast Dissolving Tablets—dissolution time <180 s, disintegration time <180 s; Fast Dissolving Films—dissolution time <60 s, disintegration time <38 s; Electrospun Nanofibers—disintegration time <1 s (fastest among all FDS due to high porosity) and dissolution time <150 s. FDT excipient ranges: superdisintegrants 5-10%, binders 1-2%. Low-volume dissolution media for films and nanofibers: 5-10 mL
ES_vs_SD_Comparative_Findings: Spray drying yields fine dry powders from aqueous drug-matrix solutions that still require compression into FDTs (disintegration <180 s, potential choking/swallowing fear). Electrospinning directly produces ultra-porous, high-surface-area nanofiber mats from just API + polymer (eliminating superdisintegrants, binders, lubricants, and fillers), converts crystalline drugs to the amorphous state via rapid solvent evaporation, enhances oral mucosal permeation and mucoadhesion, and achieves sub-second disintegration (<1 s vs <180 s for FDTs)
Limitations_and_Research_Gaps: Hygroscopicity requires moisture-barrier special packaging across FDS; bitter drugs contact taste buds requiring taste masking; both films and electrospun nanofibers suffer from inefficiency for high drug loading; FDTs carry choking concerns and hydrophobic lubricants delay disintegration; and fast-dissolving films/nanofibers require non-standard testing conditions (low-volume 5-10 mL media and high-speed camera recording)
Research_Project_Takeaway: Quantifies the disintegration advantage of electrospun nanofibers (<1 s) over spray-dried/compressed FDTs (<180 s) and cast films (<38 s) while flagging high-dose loading limits, hygroscopicity packaging, and low-volume dissolution testing needs
